items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Where mobile feels native
This week is about what *separates apps that feel native from apps that feel like a website wrapped in a shell*: **animations and gestures**. On the *web*, animation is an *enhancement* (nice-to-have). On *mobile*, it's *part of the interaction model*, the swipe to dismiss, the spring when you release a dragged element, the haptic tap on confirmation, the smooth transition. **Users feel the quality of your animations even when they can't articulate it**, fluid, responsive motion *is* much of what "feels native" means, and its absence makes an app feel cheap/web-wrapped. This week you build the *animations and gestures* that make a mobile app feel *genuinely native and alive*, the motion and touch craft that's central to mobile quality.

## Why animation and gestures are core to mobile (not enhancement)
Understanding *why* motion and gestures are *core* (not optional) on mobile frames the week:
- **They're part of the interaction model, not decoration:** on mobile, gestures (swipe, drag, pinch, long-press) and their *animated responses* (the element follows your finger, springs on release, dismisses with a swipe) *are* how you *interact* with the app, the *interaction model* is *gestural and animated*, not click-and-static. So animation/gesture isn't *added* to the interaction; it *is* the interaction (the swipe-to-dismiss, the drag, the pull-to-refresh). This is *fundamentally* different from web (where interaction is mostly clicks and animation is enhancement), on mobile, *fluid gestural interaction* is the *native* interaction model, and building it is building the *core* mobile experience.
- **Users feel the quality (even subconsciously):** users *perceive* the *quality* of animations/gestures, *even when they can't articulate it*, smooth, responsive, physical-feeling motion (springs, follows-your-finger, satisfying transitions) *feels* high-quality and native, while janky, missing, or unphysical motion *feels* cheap and "off" (even if the user can't say *why*). So the *feel* of your motion/gestures *directly* shapes the *perceived quality* of the app, subconsciously but powerfully. This is *why* native apps invest heavily in motion polish, users *feel* it. Getting the motion *right* (smooth, physical, responsive) is what makes an app *feel* premium and native.
- **It's the difference between native-feeling and web-wrapped:** the *presence and quality* of native-feeling animations/gestures is *exactly* what *separates* an app that *feels native* (fluid, gestural, alive) from one that *feels like a website in a shell* (static, clicky, web-like). So this week's skills are *the* thing that makes your React Native app feel *truly native* (vs feeling like a web app), the gestural, animated polish that *is* the native feel.
So animations and gestures are *core* to mobile (the interaction *model*, not decoration), users *feel* their quality (shaping perceived quality, even subconsciously), and they're *the difference* between native-feeling and web-wrapped, making this week's motion/gesture craft *central* to building apps that feel genuinely native.

## Where this fits
This week is animations and gestures in the Building Screens phase, *where mobile feels native*: the swipe, the spring, the haptic, the fluid motion that separate a native-feeling app from a web-wrapped one. It builds on the foundational animation polish (W3) into the full motion/gesture craft. Today's orientation: animations and gestures are *core* to mobile (the interaction model, not enhancement), users *feel* their quality (shaping perceived quality), and they're *the difference* between feeling native and feeling web-wrapped. Tomorrow you learn the modern tool: Reanimated 3.

items.title: Reanimated 3
items.body:
## Reanimated 3: performant native animation
You build animations with **Reanimated 3**, the modern, standard library for *performant* mobile animation in React Native. The key to *good* mobile animation is that it must run *smoothly* (60fps) *on the UI thread*, not blocked by JavaScript, and Reanimated achieves this by running animations *natively*:
```jsx
import Animated, { useSharedValue, useAnimatedStyle, withSpring } from 'react-native-reanimated';
function Card() {
  const scale = useSharedValue(1);
  const style = useAnimatedStyle(() => ({ transform: [{ scale: scale.value }] }));
  return <Animated.View style={style} onTouchStart={() => { scale.value = withSpring(1.1); }} />;
}
```
Reanimated uses *shared values* (`useSharedValue`, values that live on *both* JS and the UI thread) and *animated styles* (`useAnimatedStyle`, styles driven by shared values *on the UI thread*), so the animation *runs on the UI thread* (smooth, 60fps) *independent* of the JS thread. You drive shared values with animation functions (`withSpring`, `withTiming`, etc.) for physical, smooth motion.

## Why Reanimated, and the UI-thread key
Understanding *why* Reanimated (running on the UI thread) is essential for *good* mobile animation:
- **Animation must run at 60fps, on the UI thread, or it janks:** smooth animation requires *60fps* (each frame rendered in time), and if the animation is driven by the *JavaScript* thread (which is *also* doing your app's logic), a *busy* JS thread *blocks* the animation, causing *jank* (dropped frames, stutter), which *feels broken* (worse than no animation). The *fix* is to run animations on the *UI (native) thread*, *separate* from the JS thread, so they run *smoothly* (60fps) *regardless* of what the JS thread is doing. *Reanimated* does exactly this, animations run on the *UI thread* (via shared values/animated styles that live there), so they're *smooth* even when the JS thread is busy. This *UI-thread* execution is the *key* to *performant* (jank-free) mobile animation, and *why* Reanimated is the standard (the older Animated API can jank when the JS thread is busy, Reanimated doesn't).
- **Shared values and animated styles enable UI-thread animation:** Reanimated's *shared values* (live on both threads, the bridge) and *animated styles* (driven by shared values *on the UI thread*) are the *mechanism*, you define the animated value (shared value) and how styles derive from it (animated style), and Reanimated *runs* the animation on the *UI thread*, off the JS thread. Understanding this model (shared values + animated styles = UI-thread animation) is how you build performant animations. (It's a *different* mental model from regular state, the shared value is animated *natively*, not via React re-renders.)
- **It's the standard for serious mobile animation:** Reanimated is *the* library for *performant, complex* mobile animation (the older Animated API is more limited and jank-prone), so *serious* mobile animation (smooth gestures, complex transitions, the native-feel motion) is built with Reanimated. Learning it is learning *the* tool for native-feeling motion.
So Reanimated 3 is the standard for *performant* mobile animation because it runs animations on the *UI thread* (smooth 60fps, even when the JS thread is busy), via *shared values* and *animated styles*, which is the *key* to *jank-free* native-feeling motion, where janky JS-thread animation feels broken, Reanimated's UI-thread animation feels smooth and native.

## Why performant animation is non-negotiable on mobile
The deeper point is that *on mobile, animation must be performant (smooth/60fps) or it's worse than nothing*, because *janky* animation actively *feels broken* and *hurts* the perceived quality (the opposite of the native-feel goal), so *performant* animation (via Reanimated/UI-thread) is *non-negotiable* for the native feel. The whole *point* of animation on mobile is to make the app feel *fluid, responsive, native* (W6-D1), and *janky* animation *fails* that (stutter feels *cheap and broken*, worse than a static UI), so *smooth* animation is *required* for the goal. This means you *can't* just animate naively (JS-thread animation that janks under load); you *must* animate *performantly* (UI-thread, Reanimated), so the motion is *actually* smooth (delivering the native feel) rather than janky (undermining it). This is *why* Reanimated (UI-thread animation) is the *standard*, performant animation is *essential* (not optional) for mobile's native-feel goal, and Reanimated is how you achieve it. The takeaway is that *mobile animation must be performant (60fps, via UI-thread animation/Reanimated) to deliver the native feel*, because janky animation is *worse than none* (it feels broken), so you build animations with Reanimated (UI-thread, shared values, animated styles) to ensure they're *smooth*, which is *required* for the fluid, native quality that animation is *meant* to provide. Performant animation is foundational to where-mobile-feels-native, and Reanimated is the tool.

## Where this fits
You build performant animation with *Reanimated 3*: animations run on the *UI thread* (smooth 60fps, even when the JS thread is busy) via *shared values* and *animated styles*, which is the *key* to *jank-free* native-feeling motion (janky JS-thread animation is worse than none), making Reanimated the standard for serious mobile animation. Tomorrow you handle layout animations.

items.title: Layout animations
items.body:
## Layout animations: animating change automatically
A powerful, easy Reanimated feature is **layout animations**, *automatically* animating when components *appear, disappear, or move* (layout changes), so changes happen *smoothly* rather than *jarringly jumping*:
```jsx
import Animated, { FadeIn, FadeOut, Layout } from 'react-native-reanimated';
// items animate in/out and reposition smoothly as the list changes:
<Animated.View entering={FadeIn} exiting={FadeOut} layout={Layout.springify()}>
  {item.content}
</Animated.View>
```
With layout animations, you *declare* how components *enter* (`entering={FadeIn}`), *exit* (`exiting={FadeOut}`), and *reposition* (`layout={Layout}`), and Reanimated *automatically* animates these *layout changes* smoothly, an item *fading in* when added, *fading out* when removed, list items *smoothly repositioning* when the list reorders/changes, instead of *jarringly* popping in/out/jumping. This makes *dynamic* UIs (lists, conditional content, anything that changes) feel *smooth* with *minimal* code (you declare the animations; Reanimated handles them).

## Why layout animations matter (smooth change, easily)
Understanding the value of layout animations shows their impact:
- **They make *change* smooth (vs jarring jumps):** UIs *change* constantly (items added/removed from lists, content appearing/disappearing, layouts shifting), and *without* animation, these changes are *jarring* (things *pop* in/out, *jump* to new positions instantly), which feels *abrupt* and *unpolished*. *Layout animations* make these changes *smooth* (fade in/out, smooth repositioning), so the UI *flows* as it changes (the native-feel quality, smooth motion even during dynamic changes). This *smoothing of change* is a big part of what makes a UI feel *polished and native* (dynamic content that *flows* rather than *jumps*).
- **They're declarative and easy (minimal code):** the *power* of layout animations is that they're *declarative* and *automatic*, you *declare* the entering/exiting/layout animations *on* the component, and Reanimated *automatically* animates the layout changes (you don't manually orchestrate the animation). This makes *smooth dynamic UIs* achievable with *minimal* code (a few props), so you can *easily* add the polish of smooth change *everywhere* (lists, conditional content). The ease (declarative, automatic) means you *can* make *all* your dynamic UI smooth, a high polish-per-effort. So layout animations deliver smooth-change polish *easily*.
- **They're perfect for dynamic content (lists, conditionals):** layout animations shine for *dynamic content*, lists where items are added/removed/reordered (each item animates), conditional UI (content fades in/out as conditions change), anything that *appears/disappears/moves*. Since apps are *full* of dynamic content, layout animations are broadly useful for making it all feel *smooth*. For Hydra, list changes (habits, history), conditional content, etc., can all animate smoothly via layout animations.
So layout animations make *change smooth* (vs jarring jumps), *easily* (declarative, automatic, minimal code), and are *perfect for dynamic content* (lists, conditionals), a high-value, low-effort way to add the smooth-change polish that makes dynamic UIs feel *native* and *flowing* rather than *abrupt*.

## The principle: animate change for a flowing, native feel
The deeper point is that *animating *change* (transitions between states) is much of what makes a UI feel *fluid and native*, and layout animations make this *easy*, so you should *animate the changes* throughout your app for a *flowing*, *native* feel. A static UI that *jumps* between states (content appears/disappears/moves *instantly*) feels *abrupt* and *web-like*; a UI where *changes* are *animated* (smooth transitions as content appears, disappears, repositions) feels *fluid*, *continuous*, and *native* (the UI *flows* between states rather than *snapping*). So *animating change* (state transitions, content appearing/disappearing/moving) is a *core* part of the native feel, and *layout animations* make it *easy* to do *broadly* (declaratively, everywhere there's dynamic content). This means you *embrace* animating change, use layout animations to smooth the *transitions* throughout (list changes, conditional content, navigation, anything dynamic), so the *whole* app *flows* smoothly between states, which *substantially* contributes to the native feel. The takeaway is that *animating change (with layout animations) makes UIs feel fluid and native*, and since it's *easy* (declarative/automatic), you *do* it broadly, smoothing the *transitions* throughout your app so it *flows* (rather than jumps) between states, a high-value, low-effort contribution to where-mobile-feels-native. Smooth, animated *change* is a hallmark of polished native apps, and layout animations let you achieve it easily.

## Where this fits
You use *layout animations* (Reanimated's `entering`/`exiting`/`layout`) to *automatically* animate components appearing, disappearing, and moving, making *change smooth* (vs jarring jumps) *easily* (declarative, minimal code), perfect for dynamic content (lists, conditionals), because *animating change* is core to the fluid, native feel and layout animations make it easy to do broadly. Tomorrow you understand the native-driver concept deeper.

items.title: Native driver
items.body:
## The native driver: why animations stay smooth
Today you understand *deeply why* performant animation works, the **native driver** concept (which Reanimated builds on), so you can reason about animation performance. The core idea: animations should run *natively* (on the UI thread), *not* be driven frame-by-frame by JavaScript, so they stay smooth regardless of JS-thread load:
```text
JS-driven animation (jank-prone):  JS computes each frame -> if the JS thread is busy, frames drop -> jank
native-driven animation (smooth):  the animation runs NATIVELY (UI thread), JS just sets it up
                                    -> smooth 60fps EVEN IF the JS thread is busy
```
The **native driver** runs the animation *on the native/UI thread* (computing each frame *natively*), so the animation is *decoupled* from the JS thread, it runs *smoothly* even when JS is busy (doing logic, processing, etc.). This is *why* Reanimated's animations (which run natively) stay smooth, and it's the fundamental principle of performant mobile animation: *animate on the native thread, not the JS thread*.

## Why this matters: the architecture of smooth animation
Understanding the native-driver principle deeply lets you *reason about* and *ensure* animation performance:
- **The JS thread is shared and can be busy (the root problem):** in React Native, your *JavaScript* (app logic, state, rendering) runs on *one* JS thread, which can get *busy* (heavy logic, processing, re-renders), and if an *animation* is *driven* by that *same* JS thread (computing each frame in JS), a *busy* JS thread *can't* keep up with the animation's frames, causing *jank*. So the *root problem* is JS-driven animation competing with app logic on the shared JS thread. Understanding *this* (the shared, potentially-busy JS thread) explains *why* JS-driven animation janks.
- **Native-driven animation decouples it (the solution):** the *native driver* runs the animation *on the native (UI) thread*, *separate* from the JS thread, so the animation runs *independently* (smoothly, natively) *regardless* of the JS thread's load, no competing with app logic, no jank from a busy JS thread. *Decoupling* the animation from the JS thread (running it natively) is the *solution* to jank, and it's *why* native-driven (Reanimated) animations stay smooth. Understanding this *decoupling* (animation on UI thread, independent of JS) is understanding *how* smooth animation is *achieved* architecturally.
- **Some things can't be native-driven (and you must know):** *not everything* can run on the native driver, animations of *layout* properties (width, height, position via flexbox) historically couldn't (only *transform*/opacity could, with the old Animated API), though Reanimated extends what's possible. The *practical* point: you *prefer* animating the *native-drivable* properties (transform, opacity, which are also the *cheap* ones), and you *understand* that animating *expensive*/non-native-drivable properties can jank. So knowing *what* runs natively (and animating those) is part of ensuring smooth animation.
So the *native driver* principle, *run animations on the native/UI thread, decoupled from the (potentially busy) JS thread*, is the *architecture* of smooth mobile animation, understanding it (the JS-thread-is-shared problem, the native-decoupling solution, what's native-drivable) lets you *reason about* and *ensure* animation performance, building animations that *stay smooth* by running natively.

## Why understanding this matters (debugging and design)
The deeper point is that *understanding the native-driver/UI-thread principle lets you *debug* janky animations and *design* performant ones*, which is the difference between *using* animation libraries blindly and *understanding* mobile animation performance. With this understanding, when an animation *janks*, you can *reason* about *why* (is it JS-driven? is the JS thread busy? is it animating an expensive/non-native property?) and *fix* it (move it to the native driver / Reanimated, animate transform/opacity instead of layout, reduce JS-thread load), rather than being baffled. And when *designing* animations, you *choose* the performant path (native-driven, transform/opacity, Reanimated) *deliberately*, ensuring smoothness from the start. This *understanding* (vs blind library use) is what makes you able to build *reliably smooth* animations and *debug* the janky ones, a real mobile-performance competence (connecting to the mobile-performance week, W17). It's the same "understand the layer beneath the abstraction" theme, understanding *how* smooth animation works (native thread, decoupling from JS) lets you *use* the tools (Reanimated) *well* and *fix* problems, vs treating them as magic. The takeaway is that *understanding the native-driver principle (animate on the UI thread, decoupled from the JS thread) is what lets you build reliably-smooth animations and debug janky ones*, the architectural understanding that turns "use Reanimated" into "understand and ensure mobile animation performance", which is essential for delivering the consistently-smooth motion that the native feel requires. This deeper understanding is what separates competent mobile animation from cargo-culting animation libraries.

## Where this fits
You understand the *native-driver* principle deeply: animations must run on the *native/UI thread* (decoupled from the shared, potentially-busy JS thread) to stay *smooth* (60fps regardless of JS load), the *architecture* of performant mobile animation that lets you *reason about*, *ensure*, and *debug* animation performance (vs blindly using libraries), essential for consistently-smooth native-feeling motion. Tomorrow you learn common animation/gesture patterns.

items.title: Common patterns
items.body:
## Common patterns: the gestures that feel native
You learn the **common animation/gesture patterns** that *define* the native mobile feel, the swipe-to-dismiss, drag-and-drop, pull-to-refresh, the spring-on-release, the patterns users *expect* from native apps. These combine *gestures* (touch handling, via `react-native-gesture-handler`) with *animations* (Reanimated) for *fluid, physical* interactions:
```text
- swipe to dismiss/delete (swipe an item, it follows your finger, dismisses past a threshold)
- drag and drop (drag an element, it follows your finger, springs into place on release)
- pull to refresh (pull down past a threshold to refresh)
- swipeable rows (swipe to reveal actions)
- bottom sheets (drag up/down, snap to positions)
- spring physics on release (elements settle naturally, not abruptly)
- haptic feedback (a subtle vibration on confirmation/interaction)
```
You build these by *connecting gestures to animations*, the gesture (drag, swipe) *drives* a shared value (the element follows your finger via Reanimated), and on release, *physics* (spring) settles it naturally. These patterns *are* the native interaction vocabulary.

## Why these patterns matter (expected, physical, native)
Understanding why these specific patterns matter shows what makes interactions feel native:
- **Users *expect* these patterns (the native vocabulary):** native apps *all* use these patterns (swipe-to-dismiss, pull-to-refresh, drag, swipeable rows, bottom sheets), so users *expect* and *intuitively understand* them, they're the *vocabulary* of native mobile interaction. *Implementing* them (correctly) makes your app *feel native* (it speaks the expected interaction language) and *intuitive* (users *know* these gestures); *lacking* them (or implementing them poorly) makes the app feel *foreign* (web-like, missing the expected gestures). So these patterns are the *expected native interaction vocabulary*, and using them well is core to feeling native.
- **Physical motion (following the finger, spring on release) is key:** the *feel* of these patterns comes from *physicality*, the element *follows your finger* directly (1:1, responsive), and *springs* into place naturally on release (physics, not an abrupt snap or linear move). This *physical*, *responsive*, *natural* motion is what makes the gesture feel *good* (satisfying, native), vs an *unphysical* version (laggy, not following the finger, abrupt) that feels *off*. So the *physicality* (finger-following + spring physics) is *essential* to these patterns feeling native, which is *why* you build them with *gesture-driven* shared values (follows the finger) + *spring* animations (natural settling). Getting the *physics* right is what makes the gesture *feel* native.
- **Haptics add a layer of native feel:** *haptic feedback* (subtle vibration on confirmation, on hitting a threshold, on certain interactions) adds a *tactile* layer that makes interactions feel *more* native and *satisfying* (the physical *tap* of confirmation), a small but real part of the native feel that native apps use. Adding *appropriate* haptics (not overdone) enhances the native, physical feel.
So the common patterns (swipe-to-dismiss, drag, pull-to-refresh, swipeable rows, bottom sheets, with spring physics and haptics) *are* the *native interaction vocabulary* that users *expect*, and building them with *physicality* (finger-following + spring physics) and *haptics* is what makes interactions *feel native* (intuitive, physical, satisfying), vs feeling foreign or off.

## Building the native interaction vocabulary
The deeper point is that *these patterns constitute the native interaction vocabulary, and implementing them well (physically, with the expected gestures) is much of what makes an app feel genuinely native* (vs web-wrapped). The *difference* between a native-feeling app and a web-wrapped one is largely *whether it speaks the native interaction language*, the swipes, drags, pulls, sheets, springs, and haptics that users *expect* and that *feel* physical and responsive. An app that *implements these patterns well* (the expected gestures, with physical finger-following and spring physics, plus haptics) *feels native* (it interacts the way native apps do, intuitively, physically); one that *lacks* them or does them *poorly* (missing gestures, laggy/unphysical motion) *feels foreign* (web-like). So *building the native interaction vocabulary* (these patterns, done physically and correctly) is *central* to the native feel, it's *where mobile feels native* made concrete. This is *why* this week matters: implementing these gesture/animation patterns *well* is *the* thing that makes your React Native app *feel* like a *real native app* (not a website in a shell). You build them by *connecting gestures (gesture-handler) to animations (Reanimated)* with *physicality* (finger-following, spring physics) and *haptics*, the technical means to the native-feel end. The takeaway is that *the common gesture/animation patterns (swipe, drag, pull, sheets, with spring physics and haptics) are the native interaction vocabulary, and implementing them well (physically, correctly) is much of what makes an app feel genuinely native*, so mastering these patterns is mastering *where mobile feels native*. These patterns, done right, are what turn a functional app into one that *feels* native and *alive*.

## Where this fits
You learn the *common animation/gesture patterns* (swipe-to-dismiss, drag-and-drop, pull-to-refresh, swipeable rows, bottom sheets, spring physics, haptics), the *native interaction vocabulary* users expect, built by connecting *gestures* (gesture-handler) to *animations* (Reanimated) with *physicality* (finger-following + spring physics) and haptics, which is much of what makes an app feel *genuinely native* (vs web-wrapped). Tomorrow you handle pre-made complex animations with Lottie.

items.title: Lottie
items.body:
## Lottie: rich pre-made animations
For *rich, complex* animations (illustrative animations, loading animations, celebrations, onboarding illustrations) that would be hard to build by hand, you use **Lottie**, a tool/format for playing *designer-created* animations (made in After Effects, exported as JSON) in your app:
```jsx
import LottieView from 'lottie-react-native';
<LottieView source={require('./celebration.json')} autoPlay loop={false} />
```
Lottie plays *complex, designer-made* animations (a celebratory burst, an animated illustration, a rich loading spinner) from a *JSON* file (exported from After Effects by a designer/from a library), *rendered natively* and *performantly*, so you get *rich, professional* animations *without* hand-coding them. You use Lottie for the *complex, illustrative* animations (celebrations, empty-state illustrations, onboarding animations, rich loaders) where hand-building would be impractical.

## Why Lottie (complex animation made practical)
Understanding when and why to use Lottie:
- **Complex illustrative animations are impractical to hand-code:** *rich, illustrative* animations (a detailed celebration, an animated character/illustration, a complex loading animation) involve *many* moving parts, intricate timing, artistic motion, that would be *extremely* tedious (or impossible) to *hand-code* with Reanimated. *Lottie* solves this, a *designer* creates the animation (in After Effects, with full artistic control), exports it as *JSON*, and your app *plays* it (via Lottie), so you get *complex, polished* animations *without* hand-coding them. Lottie makes *rich illustrative animation practical* (designer-created, app-played). So for *complex/illustrative* animation, Lottie is the right tool (vs hand-coding).
- **It separates animation *creation* (designer) from *playing* (developer):** Lottie *separates concerns*, *designers* create the animations (their expertise, in their tools), *developers* just *play* them (a Lottie component), a clean division (like how you don't hand-code complex illustrations, you use a designer's exported assets). This *leverages* design expertise for rich animation while keeping the dev side simple (play the JSON). For polished, illustrative animation, this designer-creates-developer-plays model (Lottie) is efficient and produces *professional* results.
- **It's performant and cross-platform:** Lottie renders the animations *natively* and *performantly* (and *cross-platform*, the same JSON plays on iOS and Android), so you get *smooth*, *consistent* rich animations. So Lottie gives *rich, professional, performant, cross-platform* animations *practically*.
So Lottie makes *rich, complex, illustrative* animations *practical*, designer-created (After Effects -> JSON), developer-played (Lottie component), rendered natively and performantly, for the *complex* animations (celebrations, illustrations, rich loaders) where hand-coding is impractical, leveraging design expertise for professional results with simple developer integration.

## Choosing the right animation tool
The deeper point is *matching the animation tool to the animation type*, Reanimated/gestures for *interactive, physical* animations (the gestures, transitions, micro-interactions, where you need *code-driven, interactive* motion), and *Lottie* for *complex, illustrative, pre-made* animations (celebrations, illustrations, rich loaders, where you want *designer-created richness*), using *each* where it fits. *Reanimated* (and gesture-handler) is for the *interactive* animations, gestures that respond to touch, transitions driven by state/code, physical micro-interactions, anything *interactive* or *code-driven*. *Lottie* is for the *non-interactive, complex, illustrative* animations, rich celebrations, animated illustrations, fancy loaders, anything that's a *complex pre-made* animation. So you *choose*: interactive/physical/code-driven -> Reanimated+gestures; complex/illustrative/pre-made -> Lottie. Using *each* tool for *its* kind of animation gives you the *full* range of polished motion (interactive gestures *and* rich illustrative animations) efficiently. This is the match-the-tool-to-the-job judgment, applied to animation, *don't* hand-code a complex celebration in Reanimated (use Lottie), and *don't* try to make an interactive gesture in Lottie (use Reanimated+gestures), use *each* where it fits. The takeaway is that *you match the animation tool to the type*, Reanimated/gestures for interactive/physical/code-driven motion, Lottie for complex/illustrative/pre-made animations, using *both* (each for its purpose) to deliver the *full range* of polished mobile motion (the native interactive feel *and* rich illustrative polish) efficiently. Knowing *which* tool for *which* animation is part of mobile animation craft.

## Where this fits
You use *Lottie* for *rich, complex, illustrative* animations (celebrations, illustrations, fancy loaders), designer-created (After Effects -> JSON), developer-played (Lottie component), native and performant, for the animations where hand-coding is impractical, and you *match the animation tool to the type* (Reanimated/gestures for interactive/physical motion, Lottie for complex/illustrative pre-made animations), using both for the full range of polished motion. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship native-feeling animations and gestures.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: native-feeling animations and gestures
You assemble the week into *native-feeling* animations and gestures in Hydra (or a demo), demonstrating *where mobile feels native*:
- **performant animations** (Reanimated, UI-thread, smooth 60fps) including **layout animations** (smooth change) and **common patterns** (swipe-to-dismiss, drag, pull-to-refresh, with spring physics and haptics).
- the **native interaction vocabulary** (the expected gestures, done physically, finger-following + spring) and **Lottie** for rich illustrative animations (a celebration when you hit your hydration goal).
- everything **smooth** (UI-thread, native-driven) and **tasteful** (purposeful, not overdone, respecting reduced-motion).
```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Animations & gestures: Reanimated, native gesture patterns, Lottie - where mobile feels native"
git push
```

## The deliverable: an app that feels genuinely native
What makes this demonstrate real competence is an app that *feels genuinely native*, fluid, gestural, alive, the difference from a web-wrapped app. The strongest version has the *native interaction vocabulary* working *physically*, swipe-to-dismiss that follows your finger and springs, smooth animated transitions (layout animations making change flow), satisfying micro-interactions with haptics, a rich Lottie celebration when you hit your goal, all *smooth* (Reanimated/UI-thread, no jank) and *tasteful*. The proof is the *feel*: using the app *feels* like a *real native app* (fluid, responsive, physical gestures, smooth transitions, satisfying motion), which users *perceive* as *quality* (even subconsciously), vs a *static, clicky, web-wrapped* feel. Demonstrating that you can build the *animations and gestures that make an app feel genuinely native*, the physical gesture patterns, smooth performant motion, rich illustrative touches, is the deliverable, because this motion/gesture craft is *much* of what *separates* a native-feeling app (that users perceive as high-quality and enjoy) from a web-wrapped one (that feels cheap), it's *where mobile feels native*.

## What animations and gestures established
Step back: you have learned *where mobile feels native*, the animation and gesture craft that makes an app feel *genuinely native and alive* (vs web-wrapped). You understand that animation/gesture is *core* to mobile (the interaction *model*, and users *feel* its quality), and you can build it: *performant animation* (Reanimated, UI-thread, the native-driver principle, smooth 60fps, since janky is worse than none), *layout animations* (smooth change, easily), the *common gesture patterns* (swipe, drag, pull, sheets, with spring physics and haptics, the native interaction vocabulary, built physically by connecting gestures to animations), and *Lottie* (rich illustrative animations, matching the tool to the animation type). The throughline is that *fluid, physical, performant motion and gesture are much of what makes an app feel native*, and building them *well* (smooth, physical, using the expected patterns) is *the* craft of *where mobile feels native*, the thing that turns a functional React Native app into one that *feels* like a real native app. This is a *differentiating* mobile skill, it's what makes the difference users *feel*.

## Where this fits
You shipped native-feeling animations and gestures (Reanimated performant motion, the native gesture vocabulary with spring physics and haptics, Lottie illustrative animations), the craft of *where mobile feels native*, which separates a native-feeling app from a web-wrapped one. Next week is **theming, dark mode, and design systems**, building the consistency (a design system in code), dark-mode support (respecting the user's OS preference), and visual polish (typography, icons, type scale) that make every screen feel cohesive and professional, the systematic visual craft of mobile.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: What is the difference between useNativeDriver: true and false in React Native Animated, and why does it matter? useNativeDriver: true tells the Animated system to serialise the animation configuration and send it to the native thread once. The animation then runs entirely on the native thread without any communication back to JavaScript until it completes. This means even if the JavaScript thread is busy (loading data, running a reducer), the animation plays at 60fps. useNativeDriver: false runs the animation on the JavaScript thread, on every animation frame, JavaScript computes the new value and updates the component. Any JavaScript work pauses the animation. The constraint: useNativeDriver only works for opacity and transform. Width, height, and colour cannot use the native driver.

weeks.title: Theming, Dark Mode, and Design Systems
weeks.context:
Design systems on mobile are about consistency and speed. Every screen should feel like it belongs to the same app, same spacing scale, same colour palette, same typography, same component behaviour. A design system is not just a style guide document; it is code: a set of base components that enforce the system and make it impossible to accidentally use a spacing value that is not on the scale.

Dark mode on iOS and Android is user-controlled at the OS level. Users expect your app to respect their preference. React Native's useColorScheme hook returns 'light' or 'dark' based on the OS setting. A good dark mode is not just inverting colours, dark backgrounds should be very dark grey (#121212 or #1C1C1E) not pure black (#000000), and text should be slightly off-white (#E1E1E1) not pure white (#FFFFFF). Pure black on pure white feels harsh.

Theming architecture: define your design tokens as a TypeScript object, colours, spacing, typography, border radii. Create a light theme and a dark theme. Expose the current theme via a React context (ThemeContext) so any component can access it. Many teams use a custom hook: const { colors, spacing } = useTheme(). The alternative is a theming library, react-native-paper or NativeWind (Tailwind for React Native).

Typography: mobile apps should have a small, coherent set of text styles. Define them explicitly: header (24px, bold), title (18px, semibold), body (14px, regular), caption (12px, regular). Apply them via a Text component that accepts a variant prop. The OS handles the base font, San Francisco on iOS, Roboto on Android. If you need a custom font, use expo-font. Keep it to two weights maximum, loading many font files increases startup time.

Spacing scale: use multiples of 4 or 8 as your spacing unit. spacing.xs = 4, spacing.sm = 8, spacing.md = 16, spacing.lg = 24, spacing.xl = 32. Never use arbitrary values like padding: 13, it breaks the visual rhythm. Standardising spacing is the single highest-impact thing you can do for visual consistency without a designer.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Design systems on mobile: consistency and speed
This week is about **theming, dark mode, and design systems**, the systematic visual craft that makes *every screen feel like it belongs to the same app*. A **design system** on mobile is about *consistency and speed*: every screen should share the *same* spacing scale, colour palette, typography, and component behaviour, so the app feels *cohesive* and *professional*. Crucially, a design system is *not just a style-guide document; it is code*, a set of *base components* and *design tokens* that *enforce* the system (making it *impossible* to accidentally use an off-scale value). This week you build a design system *in code* (tokens, themed components), add *dark mode* (respecting the user's OS preference), and handle typography/icons, the systematic approach to consistent, polished mobile visuals.

## Why a design system (consistency + speed), and as code
Understanding *why* a design system matters, and why *as code*, frames the week:
- **Consistency makes the app feel cohesive and professional:** when *every* screen uses the *same* spacing, colours, typography, and components, the app feels like *one cohesive, professional* product; when screens are *inconsistent* (different spacings, slightly-different colours, varied typography), it feels *amateur* and *disjointed* (even if each screen is individually fine). So *consistency* (a shared design system) is what makes the app feel *cohesive and quality*, the same designed-look-from-consistency principle as web (W3 of full-stack), now systematized for mobile. A design system *ensures* this consistency across all screens.
- **A design system as *code* *enforces* consistency (vs a doc that's ignored):** a design system as a *document* (a style guide) is *easily ignored* (developers don't follow it, drift creeps in), but a design system as *code* (design *tokens* and *base components* that *embody* the system) *enforces* it, if you build screens from *themed base components* using *design tokens* (not arbitrary values), you *can't* accidentally be inconsistent (you *use* the system's spacing/colours/components, so consistency is *automatic*). So a design system *in code* (tokens + base components) makes consistency *enforced and effortless* (you build from the system) rather than *aspirational and ignored* (a doc). This *code-not-doc* point is key, the system is *enforced* by being the *components/tokens you build with*.
- **It speeds development:** building from a *design system* (reusable themed components, defined tokens) is *faster*, you *compose* screens from existing themed components (not styling each from scratch), with consistent tokens (not deciding values each time), so development is *faster* and *consistent*. The design system is a *productivity* tool (build faster from the system) *and* a consistency tool. So a design system delivers *both consistency and speed*.
So a design system matters because *consistency makes the app cohesive/professional*, and a design system *as code* (tokens + base components) *enforces* that consistency (vs an ignored doc) *and* *speeds* development (build from the system), delivering the *consistency and speed* that make a polished, cohesive mobile app efficiently.

## Where this fits
This week is theming/dark-mode/design-systems in the Building Screens phase: the systematic visual craft (a design system *in code*, dark mode, typography, icons) that makes every screen *cohesive and professional*. Today's orientation: a design system is about *consistency and speed*, and crucially it's *code* (design tokens + base components that *enforce* the system), not just a document, delivering cohesion (consistency) and faster development (build from the system). Tomorrow you build the foundation: design tokens.

items.title: Design tokens
items.body:
## Design tokens: the system's values in code
The foundation of a design-system-in-code is **design tokens**, the *named, defined values* (colours, spacing, typography, radii, etc.) that the system uses, defined *once* in code and *used* everywhere (instead of arbitrary hard-coded values):
```jsx
// design tokens - the system's values, defined once:
export const tokens = {
  color: { bg: '#fff', text: '#1a1a1a', primary: '#3b82f6', ... },
  space: { xs: 4, sm: 8, md: 16, lg: 24, xl: 32 },     // the spacing scale
  radius: { sm: 6, md: 12, lg: 20 },
  font: { size: { sm: 14, md: 16, lg: 20, xl: 28 }, weight: { ... } },
};
// used everywhere (not arbitrary values):
<View style={{ padding: tokens.space.md, backgroundColor: tokens.color.bg }} />
```
You *define* the system's values as *tokens* (named: `space.md`, `color.primary`, `font.size.lg`) *once*, and *use* the tokens *everywhere* (not arbitrary `padding: 17`), so *all* the values come from the *defined system*. This *centralizes* the design values (one source of truth) and *enforces* using the *system's* values (the scale, the palette) rather than arbitrary ones.

## Why design tokens (single source, enforced scale)
Understanding the value of tokens shows why they're foundational:
- **Single source of truth (change once, everywhere):** tokens *centralize* the design values, the colours, spacing, type sizes are *defined once* (the tokens) and *referenced* everywhere, so *changing* a value (the primary colour, a spacing) is *one edit* (the token), updating it *everywhere*. This *single-source-of-truth* makes the design *maintainable* and *consistent* (one place defines each value, used uniformly), vs scattered hard-coded values (inconsistent, change-everywhere). Tokens give *centralized, maintainable* design values.
- **They *enforce* the scale/palette (consistency by construction):** by *using* tokens (the defined *scale* of spacings, the *palette* of colours), you *can only* use the *system's* values (you reference `space.md`, not type `17`), so consistency is *enforced by construction*, you *can't* (easily) use an off-scale value, because you build from the *tokens* (the scale). This is the *code-enforces-consistency* point, tokens *make* you use the system's values, so the design *stays* consistent (the spacing is *always* on the scale, the colours *always* from the palette). Tokens enforce the *constrained design system* (the same constrained-choices-give-consistency idea as Tailwind on web), in code.
- **They're the foundation for theming (e.g. dark mode):** tokens are *also* the foundation for *theming* (D3, dark mode), you define *light* and *dark* token *values*, and switch the *token set* based on the theme, so the *whole* app re-themes by swapping tokens. So tokens *enable* theming (light/dark) cleanly (swap the token values). Tokens are the foundation for both *consistency* and *theming*.
So design tokens, the system's values defined *once* in code and used everywhere, give a *single source of truth* (change once, everywhere, maintainable), *enforce* the scale/palette (consistency by construction, you build from the tokens), and are the *foundation for theming* (light/dark token sets), the foundational building block of a design-system-in-code.

## Tokens as the foundation of systematic design
The deeper point is that *design tokens are the foundation of *systematic* design, turning ad-hoc styling into a coherent, enforced, maintainable system*. Without tokens, styling is *ad-hoc* (arbitrary values scattered everywhere, inconsistent, hard to change, no system), with tokens, styling becomes *systematic* (all values from a *defined* set, consistent by construction, maintainable from one source, themeable). Tokens are what *make* the design a *system* (a coherent, defined, enforced set of values) rather than a *pile* of arbitrary styles. This *systematization* (via tokens) is what delivers the design system's benefits, *consistency* (everything uses the system's values), *maintainability* (change the tokens), *theming* (swap token sets), and *speed* (build from defined values, no per-decision agonizing). So building tokens *first* is building the *foundation* of the systematic design that the rest follows (themed base components built *from* tokens, theming *via* tokens). For mobile (and any app), this *token-based systematic design* is the professional approach, define the system's values as tokens, build everything from them, getting consistency, maintainability, themeability, and speed. The takeaway is that *design tokens are the foundation of systematic design*, the defined, single-source, enforced values that turn ad-hoc styling into a coherent, consistent, maintainable, themeable system, so you build them first as the basis for the design-system-in-code. Tokens are where systematic, professional mobile visual design starts.

## Where this fits
You build *design tokens*, the system's values (colours, spacing, typography, radii) defined *once* in code and used everywhere, giving a *single source of truth* (change once, everywhere), *enforcing* the scale/palette (consistency by construction), and forming the *foundation for theming*, the foundational building block that turns ad-hoc styling into a coherent, systematic, maintainable design. Tomorrow you add dark mode with useColorScheme.

items.title: useColorScheme
items.body:
## Dark mode: respecting the user's preference
You add **dark mode**, which on mobile is *user-controlled at the OS level* (users set light/dark in their device settings and *expect* apps to *respect* it). React Native's **`useColorScheme`** hook tells you the OS preference, and you switch your *token set* accordingly:
```jsx
import { useColorScheme } from 'react-native';
const scheme = useColorScheme();              // 'light' or 'dark' (the OS setting)
const theme = scheme === 'dark' ? darkTokens : lightTokens;   // swap the token set
// the whole app uses `theme` tokens -> re-themes automatically with the OS setting
```
You define *light* and *dark* token sets (the values for each theme, built on D2's tokens), use `useColorScheme` to get the OS preference, and *apply* the matching token set, so the app *automatically* matches the user's OS light/dark setting. Because everything uses *tokens* (D2), swapping the token set *re-themes the whole app* cleanly.

## Doing dark mode *well* (not just inverting)
Understanding *good* dark mode (a real craft) is the key lesson:
- **Respect the OS preference (users expect it):** dark mode is *user-controlled at the OS level*, and users *expect* apps to *respect* their choice (if their phone is in dark mode, your app should be too), so you *follow* the OS setting (`useColorScheme`) by default, *respecting* their preference (the respect-the-user theme, and a strong user expectation). An app that *ignores* the OS dark-mode setting (always light) feels *wrong* (it doesn't respect the user's choice). So respecting the OS preference is the baseline.
- **Good dark mode is *designed*, not just inverted:** a *good* dark mode is *not* just *inverting* colours, it's *designed*. Key craft: dark backgrounds should be *very dark grey* (`#121212`, `#1C1C1E`) *not pure black* (`#000000`) (pure black is harsh, and on OLED can cause smearing; dark grey is softer, more refined), text should be *off-white* (not pure white, which is harsh on dark), and you *adjust* colours for dark (saturated colours may need toning, contrast must be maintained), elevation/depth is shown differently (lighter surfaces for "raised", not shadows). So *good* dark mode *designs* the dark theme (proper dark-grey backgrounds, off-white text, adjusted colours, dark-appropriate depth), not a naive inversion. This *dark-mode craft* (the specific dos: dark grey not black, off-white not white, adjusted colours, maintained contrast) is what makes dark mode look *good* (refined) vs *bad* (harsh, naive-inverted).
- **Tokens make it clean (swap the set):** because you use *tokens* (D2), implementing dark mode is *clean*, define *dark* token *values* (the well-designed dark colours) and *swap* the token set based on `useColorScheme`, and the *whole* app re-themes (everything uses tokens). So tokens *enable* clean theming (define light/dark token sets, swap them), which is *why* tokens are the foundation for theming, dark mode is "just" a different token set, applied everywhere via the tokens.
So good dark mode means *respecting the OS preference* (`useColorScheme`, users expect it), *designing* the dark theme well (dark grey not black, off-white not white, adjusted colours, maintained contrast, the dark-mode craft, not naive inversion), implemented *cleanly* via *token sets* (define dark tokens, swap based on the OS setting, re-theming the whole app). Good dark mode is *designed and respectful*, not just inverted.

## Why dark mode matters (expectation, comfort, craft)
The deeper point is that *dark mode is an expected, comfort-affecting feature that, done *well*, signals quality and respect, while done *poorly* (or absent) signals the opposite*. Dark mode is *expected* (a standard feature users look for and use), it affects *comfort* (dark mode is easier on the eyes in low light, preferred by many), and it's *user-controlled* (respecting their OS choice is respecting them). So *supporting* it (respecting the OS preference) is meeting an *expectation* and *respecting* the user, and supporting it *well* (a properly-*designed* dark theme, not a harsh naive inversion) *signals quality* (the refined dark mode shows care), while a *bad* dark mode (harsh pure-black, harsh white text, broken contrast) or *no* dark mode signals *lack of care* (or ignores the user's preference). This connects to the polish/perceived-quality and respect-the-user themes, dark mode done *well* is part of a *polished, respectful, quality* app. Tokens make doing it *well* *practical* (clean theming via token sets), so there's little excuse not to. For Hydra, a well-designed dark mode (respecting the OS, with proper dark-grey/off-white design) makes it *comfortable* (usable in low light, the bedside-hydration-check) and *polished* (refined dark theme). The takeaway is that *dark mode is an expected, comfort-affecting feature to do *well* (respect the OS preference, *design* the dark theme properly, implemented cleanly via tokens), because good dark mode signals quality and respect while bad/absent dark mode signals the opposite*, and tokens make doing it well practical. Good dark mode is part of polished, respectful mobile design.

## Where this fits
You add *dark mode* (user-controlled at the OS level via `useColorScheme`, which users expect you to respect), done *well*, *designed* (dark grey not pure black, off-white not pure white, adjusted colours, maintained contrast, not naive inversion), implemented *cleanly* via *token sets* (swap light/dark tokens, re-theming the whole app), because good dark mode signals quality and respect (an expected, comfort-affecting feature). Tomorrow you handle custom fonts.

items.title: Custom fonts
items.body:
## Custom fonts: typography that's yours
You add **custom fonts**, loading and using brand/custom typefaces (rather than only the system default), which is part of a distinctive, polished visual identity:
```jsx
import { useFonts } from 'expo-font';
const [loaded] = useFonts({
  'Inter-Regular': require('./assets/fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf'),
  'Inter-Bold': require('./assets/fonts/Inter-Bold.ttf'),
});
if (!loaded) return null;       // wait for fonts to load
// use them via tokens: fontFamily: 'Inter-Bold'
```
You *load* custom font files (via `expo-font`), *wait* for them to load (showing a splash/nothing until ready, so text doesn't flash in the wrong font), and *use* them (via your typography tokens, so the system's fonts are consistent). Custom fonts give your app a *distinctive*, *intentional* typographic identity (vs the generic system font), part of a cohesive, branded, polished design.

## Why typography (and custom fonts) matters
Understanding why typography is so important to visual quality:
- **Typography is a huge part of visual identity and quality:** *typography* (the fonts, their sizes, weights, spacing) is a *major* component of an app's *visual identity* and *perceived quality*, good, intentional typography (a well-chosen font, consistent sizing/weighting) makes an app look *designed, distinctive, professional*, while default/inconsistent typography looks *generic*. So *typography* is a *high-impact* part of the visual design, and *custom fonts* (an intentional typeface) are part of a *distinctive, quality* look. Investing in typography (custom fonts, a type scale, D6) significantly elevates the visual quality.
- **Font loading must be handled (avoid the flash/wrong-font):** custom fonts must be *loaded* (async, the font files load), and you must *handle* the loading, *wait* for the fonts before rendering text (else text *flashes* in the *default* font then *swaps* to the custom one, a jarring "flash of unstyled/wrong text", the same FOUT issue as web). So you *wait* for fonts to load (`useFonts`, show a splash until ready) so text renders in the *correct* font from the start. Handling font loading (waiting, avoiding the flash) is the technical care that makes custom fonts look *right* (no jarring swap). This is the loading-experience detail (like the dark-mode flash from W2 of full-stack), handled.
- **Custom fonts integrate with the design system (tokens):** you use the custom fonts *via* the typography *tokens* (D2), so the fonts are part of the *consistent system* (the type tokens specify the custom fonts, used everywhere), keeping typography consistent. So custom fonts fit into the token-based design system (the type tokens use them).
So custom fonts matter because *typography is a major part of visual identity and quality* (intentional fonts make an app look designed/distinctive/professional vs generic), and using them requires *handling font loading* (waiting to avoid the flash-of-wrong-font) and *integrating with the design system* (via type tokens for consistency). Custom, well-handled typography significantly elevates the app's visual quality and identity.

## Typography as a pillar of design
The deeper point is that *typography is a *pillar* of visual design, and treating it systematically (custom fonts, a type scale, consistent usage via tokens) is part of a professional, cohesive visual identity*. Alongside colour and spacing, *typography* is one of the *core pillars* of visual design, and a *cohesive, intentional* typography (a chosen typeface, a consistent type scale of sizes/weights, D6, applied uniformly via tokens) is *essential* to a *polished, branded, professional* look. *Amateur* design often neglects typography (default fonts, inconsistent/arbitrary sizes), while *professional* design *systematizes* it (intentional fonts, a defined type scale, consistent application), which is a *major* part of why professional apps *look* professional. So you treat typography as a *first-class* design concern, *custom fonts* (intentional typeface, well-loaded), a *type scale* (defined sizes/weights, D6), applied *consistently* (via tokens), making typography part of the *systematic design* (not an afterthought). For Hydra, intentional typography (a clean custom font, consistent sizing) elevates its visual identity toward professional polish. The takeaway is that *typography is a pillar of visual design that you treat systematically* (custom fonts well-handled, a consistent type scale, applied via tokens), because intentional, cohesive typography is a *major* part of a professional, distinctive, polished visual identity, neglecting it (default/inconsistent type) is a common amateur-design failing, and systematizing it is part of professional mobile design. Good typography, systematized, is foundational to visual quality.

## Where this fits
You add *custom fonts* (intentional typefaces via `expo-font`, with *font loading handled*, waiting to avoid the flash-of-wrong-font, integrated via type tokens), because *typography is a major pillar of visual identity and quality* (intentional fonts make an app look designed/professional vs generic), treated *systematically* (custom fonts, type scale, consistent application) as part of a cohesive, professional design. Tomorrow you handle icons.

items.title: Icons
items.body:
## Icons: consistent, scalable iconography
You add **icons**, the small symbols (navigation, actions, status) that are essential to mobile UI, using an *icon system* (a consistent icon set, scalable, themeable):
```jsx
import { Ionicons } from '@expo/vector-icons';   // a built-in icon set
<Ionicons name="water" size={24} color={theme.color.primary} />
```
You use a *vector icon set* (like `@expo/vector-icons`, which bundles popular icon sets, or a custom set), giving *consistent*, *scalable* (vector, crisp at any size), *themeable* (colour via props/tokens) icons. Icons are *everywhere* in mobile UI (tab bars, buttons, lists, status), so a *consistent icon system* (one cohesive icon set, used uniformly, themed via tokens) is part of the cohesive design. You use icons consistently (from one set, sized/coloured via the design system).

## Why an icon system (consistency, clarity, scalability)
Understanding the value of a consistent icon system:
- **Icons are essential to mobile UI (ubiquitous, space-efficient):** icons are *everywhere* in mobile (tab bars, action buttons, list items, status indicators), because they're *space-efficient* (a small icon conveys meaning without text, valuable on small screens) and *quickly recognizable* (a familiar icon is instantly understood). So icons are a *core, ubiquitous* part of mobile UI, and handling them *well* (a good icon system) matters. Good iconography is essential to mobile UI.
- **Consistency (one cohesive set) is key:** using a *consistent* icon set (icons that share a *style*, all from one cohesive set) makes the UI feel *cohesive and professional*, while *mixing* icon styles (different sets, inconsistent styles) looks *disjointed and amateur*. So you use *one cohesive icon set* (consistent style throughout), part of the design-system consistency. Icon *consistency* (one set, one style) is the key, the same consistency principle as colours/spacing/typography, applied to icons.
- **Vector icons scale and theme cleanly:** *vector* icons (like the icon-font/SVG sets) are *scalable* (crisp at *any* size, no pixelation, vs raster images) and *themeable* (you set their *colour* via props, so they match the theme/tokens, including dark mode). So vector icons are the *right* approach (scalable, themeable, integrating with the design system, colour via tokens, crisp at any size). Using a vector icon set (sized and coloured via the design system) gives clean, consistent, themeable iconography.
So an icon system matters because *icons are essential and ubiquitous* in mobile UI (space-efficient, recognizable), *consistency* (one cohesive set/style) is key to a cohesive professional look (vs disjointed mixed icons), and *vector* icons (scalable, themeable via tokens) are the right approach (crisp at any size, matching the theme). A consistent, vector, design-system-integrated icon system is part of cohesive, polished mobile UI.

## Icons as part of the cohesive design system
The deeper point is that *icons are part of the *design system*, and treating them systematically (one consistent set, integrated with tokens/theming) is part of the cohesive visual consistency*. Just as colours, spacing, and typography are part of the design system (tokens, consistent usage), *icons* are *also* a design-system concern, you choose *one* cohesive icon set (consistent style), use it *uniformly* (the same set throughout, not mixing), and *integrate* it with the design system (icons sized via spacing tokens, coloured via colour tokens, so they match the theme including dark mode). This makes icons part of the *consistent, cohesive* design (not an inconsistent afterthought). So you treat icons *systematically* (one set, consistent usage, token-integrated), part of the *overall* design-system consistency (colours + spacing + typography + icons, all systematic and cohesive). This systematic treatment of *all* the visual elements (including icons) is what makes the *whole* app feel *cohesive and professional* (everything, including the icons, is consistent and on-system). For Hydra, a consistent icon set (one cohesive style, themed via tokens, water/habit-related icons) is part of its cohesive visual identity. The takeaway is that *icons are part of the design system, treated systematically* (one consistent cohesive set, vector/scalable, integrated with tokens/theming for consistent sizing/colouring), as part of the *overall* visual consistency (with colours, spacing, typography) that makes the app cohesive and professional. Systematic iconography is part of the cohesive design system, completing the visual consistency across all elements.

## Where this fits
You add *icons* via a consistent *vector icon set* (`@expo/vector-icons` or custom), *essential and ubiquitous* in mobile UI (space-efficient, recognizable), used *consistently* (one cohesive set/style) and *integrated* with the design system (scalable, themed via tokens including dark mode), part of the *overall* systematic visual consistency (colours + spacing + typography + icons) that makes the app cohesive and professional. items.title: Type scale
items.body:
## The type scale: systematic typography sizing
You build a **type scale**, a *defined set* of font sizes (and weights) used *consistently* throughout, the systematic approach to typography sizing (vs arbitrary sizes):
```jsx
// a type scale (defined sizes, in your tokens):
font: { size: { caption: 12, body: 16, subtitle: 20, title: 28, hero: 36 }, ... }
// used semantically (not arbitrary sizes):
<Text style={{ fontSize: tokens.font.size.title }}>...</Text>   // a "title"
<Text style={{ fontSize: tokens.font.size.body }}>...</Text>    // "body" text
```
A *type scale* is a *limited, harmonious* set of font sizes (e.g. caption/body/subtitle/title/hero, a defined progression), used *semantically* (you use "title" or "body", not arbitrary `fontSize: 22`), so *all* text uses the *scale's* sizes (consistent typography). This *constrains* type sizes to the *defined scale* (like the spacing scale for spacing), giving *consistent, harmonious* typography.

## Why a type scale (consistency, hierarchy, harmony)
Understanding the value of a type scale:
- **It enforces consistent type sizes (like the spacing scale):** a type scale *constrains* font sizes to a *defined set* (the scale), so you *use* the scale's sizes (body, title, etc.) *not* arbitrary values (`fontSize: 22` here, `21` there), giving *consistent* typography across the app (the *same* sizes used uniformly). This is the *constrained-scale-gives-consistency* principle (as for spacing, D2, and Tailwind on web), applied to *type sizes*, the scale *enforces* consistent sizing. So a type scale gives *consistent* type sizes (no arbitrary, slightly-different sizes scattered around).
- **It creates clear hierarchy:** a *good* type scale has *distinct*, *purposeful* sizes (caption < body < subtitle < title < hero) that create clear *visual hierarchy* (headings stand out from body, the size progression guides the eye), so the typography *communicates structure* (what's a heading, what's body, what's emphasized). Using the scale *semantically* (title for titles, body for body) creates this clear hierarchy. So the type scale gives *clear typographic hierarchy* (purposeful size distinctions that structure the content). Good hierarchy aids readability and looks professional.
- **It's harmonious (the sizes relate well):** a *well-designed* type scale has sizes that *relate harmoniously* (often a ratio-based progression), so the sizes *look good together* (harmonious, balanced) vs arbitrary sizes (which can clash or look haphazard). So the scale gives *harmonious* typography (sizes that work well together). A harmonious type scale looks *designed* (vs arbitrary sizes looking accidental).
So a type scale matters because it *enforces consistent type sizes* (the constrained-scale principle, no arbitrary sizes), creates *clear hierarchy* (purposeful, distinct sizes used semantically, structuring content), and is *harmonious* (sizes that relate well, looking designed), giving *consistent, hierarchical, harmonious* typography, the systematic approach that makes typography look professional and cohesive.

## Completing the systematic design
The deeper point is that *the type scale completes the systematic, token-based design, where *every* visual dimension (colour, spacing, typography sizing, icons) is *systematic* (defined, constrained, consistent), which is what makes the whole app cohesively professional*. With the type scale, you now have *all* the visual dimensions *systematized*: *colour* (a defined palette in tokens, with light/dark themes), *spacing* (a defined scale), *typography* (custom fonts + a defined type scale), and *icons* (a consistent set), all *defined* (tokens), *constrained* (scales/palettes/sets), and *consistent* (used uniformly via the system). This *complete systematization* of the visual design is what delivers a *cohesively professional* app, *everything* (colours, spacing, type, icons) is *on-system* (consistent, harmonious, intentional), so the *whole* app feels *cohesive, designed, and professional*. This is the *full design-system-in-code*, tokens defining all the values, base components and consistent usage enforcing the system, across *all* visual dimensions, which gives both the *consistency* (cohesive look) and *speed* (build from the system) the week is about. For Hydra, this complete design system (consistent colour/spacing/type/icons, themed for dark mode) makes *every* screen feel like *one cohesive, polished, professional* app. The takeaway is that *the type scale completes the systematic design, where every visual dimension (colour, spacing, typography, icons) is systematized (defined, constrained, consistent) via the design-system-in-code*, which is what makes the whole app *cohesively professional* (everything on-system), delivering the consistency and speed of a real design system. Systematizing *all* the visual dimensions is the essence of professional, cohesive mobile visual design.

## Where this fits
You build a *type scale* (a defined, harmonious set of font sizes used semantically and consistently), which *enforces consistent type sizes* (the constrained-scale principle), creates *clear hierarchy*, and is *harmonious*, *completing* the systematic token-based design where *every* visual dimension (colour, spacing, typography, icons) is systematized (defined, constrained, consistent), making the whole app cohesively professional. Tomorrow you assemble the week and ship the themed design system.

You understand that a design system is about *consistency and speed* and is *code* (not a doc), and you can build it: *design tokens* (the single-source, constrained, themeable values), *dark mode* done well (respecting the OS preference, *designing* the dark theme, via token sets), *custom fonts* (intentional, well-loaded typography), *icons* (a consistent vector set), and a *type scale* (consistent, hierarchical, harmonious sizing), all *systematized* (defined, constrained, consistent, themeable) across *every* visual dimension. items.body: A user's device is in dark mode. Your app does not respond to it, it always shows the light theme. What is wrong? All colour values in your components come from the theme, not hardcoded.

weeks.title: Local Storage, AsyncStorage, MMKV, SQLite
weeks.context:
Data that does not persist across app restarts is data the user has to re-enter. Local storage is how mobile apps remember state. There are three levels of local storage, each with different characteristics, and choosing the wrong one for your use case causes performance problems or data loss.

AsyncStorage is a simple key-value store backed by the device's file system. It is asynchronous (reads and writes are non-blocking I/O operations). It stores strings, you JSON.stringify objects before storing and JSON.parse after reading. It has no schema, no queries, and no transactions. Appropriate for: small amounts of configuration data (user preferences, theme setting, reminder time), simple flags (has the user seen the onboarding?). Not appropriate for: large datasets, structured data you want to query, data that updates frequently.

MMKV is a key-value store that works via memory-mapped files, reads are synchronous (no await required) and extremely fast (microseconds vs milliseconds). It uses the same API pattern as AsyncStorage but synchronously. Install via expo-community-flipper or react-native-mmkv. Appropriate for: same use cases as AsyncStorage, but where synchronous access is important (accessing values inside gesture handlers or worklets) or where you have many small reads.

SQLite is a relational database embedded in your app. It supports SQL queries, indexes, transactions, foreign keys, and can handle millions of rows efficiently. Reads and writes are asynchronous. Covered in W3. Appropriate for: structured data you need to query (habit history, order history, cached API responses).

Secure storage: AsyncStorage and MMKV store data in plaintext on the device. For sensitive data (auth tokens, API keys, biometric-protected secrets), use expo-secure-store, which uses iOS Keychain and Android Keystore, OS-level secure enclaves. Always store user credentials and tokens in secure storage.

This week you audit Hydra's storage: move all simple settings to MMKV (synchronous, fast), keep the completion history in SQLite, and move the auth token (if you add authentication) to expo-secure-store.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## How mobile apps remember: the storage levels
This week is the *full* picture of **local storage**, how mobile apps *remember* state. The premise: *data that doesn't persist across app restarts is data the user has to re-enter*, so local storage is essential. There are **three levels of local storage**, each with different characteristics, and *choosing the wrong one causes performance problems or data loss*:
```text
AsyncStorage:  simple key-value, async, strings - for small config/preferences
MMKV:          fast key-value, synchronous - for frequently-accessed key-value data (fast)
SQLite:        a real relational database - for structured, queryable data
```
You've met AsyncStorage (W1) and SQLite (W3); this week you understand *all three* (adding MMKV), their *characteristics*, and crucially *how to choose* the right one, because the wrong choice causes real problems (slow performance, or data loss). This is the *storage-categorization* skill (like the web track's state categories) for mobile: match the storage tool to the data.

## The three levels, and why choosing right matters
Understanding the three storage levels and their fit frames the week:
- **AsyncStorage, simple key-value, for small config:** AsyncStorage is a *simple key-value* store (backed by the file system), *asynchronous* (non-blocking I/O), storing *strings* (JSON.stringify objects), with *no schema, queries, or transactions*. It's *appropriate* for *small* amounts of *configuration* data (preferences, theme, reminder time) and *simple flags* (has-seen-onboarding). It's *not* appropriate for large or structured data. So AsyncStorage is for *small, simple* key-value data.
- **MMKV, fast key-value, for frequent access:** MMKV is a *fast* key-value store (much faster than AsyncStorage), and notably *synchronous* (instant reads/writes, no await), so it's *appropriate* for key-value data accessed *frequently* or needed *synchronously* (where AsyncStorage's async overhead is a problem). It's the *fast* key-value option. So MMKV is for *frequently-accessed* (or sync-needed) *key-value* data, where speed matters.
- **SQLite, a real database, for structured data:** SQLite is a *real relational database* (tables, SQL queries, transactions), for *structured, queryable* data (history, records, complex data, W3). It's the tool for *structured* data you want to *query*. So SQLite is for *structured, queryable* data.
- **Choosing wrong causes problems:** using the *wrong* tool causes *real problems*, structured data in AsyncStorage (awkward, slow as it grows, W3's lesson), or frequently-accessed data in slow AsyncStorage (performance), or simple config in a heavyweight SQLite (overkill). So *choosing right* (matching the tool to the data: simple-small -> AsyncStorage, fast-key-value -> MMKV, structured -> SQLite) *matters* (the wrong choice causes performance issues or awkwardness/data-loss). Matching storage to data is the key skill.
So the three storage levels, *AsyncStorage* (simple small key-value), *MMKV* (fast key-value), *SQLite* (structured queryable data), each fit *different* data, and *choosing right* (matching tool to data) *matters* (wrong choice = performance problems or awkwardness), the storage-categorization skill the week builds.

## Where this fits
This week completes the Building Screens phase with the *full* local-storage picture: the three levels (AsyncStorage, MMKV, SQLite), their characteristics, and *choosing the right one* (since the wrong choice causes performance problems or data loss), plus storage concerns (migrations, encryption, backup). Today's orientation: mobile apps *remember* via local storage, there are *three levels* (AsyncStorage simple-small key-value, MMKV fast key-value, SQLite structured data), and *choosing the right one matters* (match the tool to the data). Tomorrow you revisit AsyncStorage in depth.
