items.title: iOS vs Android notification UX
items.body:
## iOS vs Android notification UX: making push feel native on both
A notification that's tuned for iOS can feel *foreign* on Android and vice-versa. The two platforms present, group, and control notifications *differently*, and respecting those differences is what makes push feel *native* rather than ported. Today is the cross-platform polish.

## The key differences
```text
                 iOS                         Android
Permission   Must REQUEST (opt-in).      Granted by default <13; Android 13+ also
                                          requires a runtime request.
Grouping     By app, threads by          By CHANNEL; user controls each channel's
             'threadId'.                  importance/sound/on-off independently.
Importance   Provisional auth +          Channel importance (HIGH = heads-up banner,
             interruption levels         DEFAULT, LOW, MIN) set per channel.
             (passive..time-sensitive).
Badge        App-icon number (you set    Often a DOT; numeric badges vary by launcher.
             'badge'; you manage count).
Rich UI      Notification Service Ext.    Expandable layouts, action buttons,
             for images/attachments.     custom styles.
```
The two big takeaways: **iOS centres on permission + interruption level + badge counts**, while **Android centres on channels** (the user's granular control surface). Design for *both* models, not one.

## Practical cross-platform rules
- **Request permission well on iOS:** ask *in context* after showing the value ("turn on reminders to hit your goal"), not on first launch, opt-in rates plummet with a cold prompt. Consider iOS *provisional* authorisation (notifications arrive quietly to the Notification Center without a prompt) to earn trust before asking for full permission.
- **Use Android channels meaningfully (D3):** they're the user's tuning knobs, separate "reminders" from "tips" so users mute the noise, not you entirely.
- **Manage the iOS badge count honestly:** a "1" that never clears is annoying; update/clear the badge as the user reads things.
- **Test on *both* real devices:** notification behaviour is one of the *least* faithful things in simulators/emulators. *iOS push doesn't even work in the simulator.* Always verify on physical hardware, both platforms.

## Respect "Time-Sensitive" and Do Not Disturb
iOS *interruption levels* and Android *importance* decide whether you can break through Focus/DND. *Reserve high-urgency/time-sensitive for genuinely time-critical pushes* (a security code, a live alert), abusing it to force a marketing nudge through DND is exactly the abuse that gets you disabled.

Today: tune Hydra's notifications per platform, in-context iOS permission (consider provisional), meaningful Android channels, honest badge handling, and verify the *same* notification on a real iPhone *and* a real Android, noting how each presents it. Platform-respectful push is the difference between "native" and "ported".

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: Hydra v0.7, push notifications done right
Package the week into **Hydra v0.7**: a notification system that *re-engages* users with *relevant, controllable, cross-platform-native* pushes, the kind users keep enabled because they're genuinely useful, not the kind they mute on day two.

## What v0.7 must demonstrate
- **Permission + token, robust:** in-context permission request, Expo push token fetched, sent to a backend (or mocked), and *refreshed on launch* (tokens rotate).
- **Local + remote, used correctly:** fixed reminders as *local* notifications; server-computed nudges as *remote* pushes, each used for what it's for.
- **Targeted server sends:** a *timezone-aware, personalised* reminder to users behind their goal (real or sketched backend), pruning dead tokens via receipts.
- **Polished client handling:** foreground handler, Android channels, and *tap deep-linking* via the `data` payload to the right screen.
- **Cross-platform native feel:** verified on a *real* iPhone and a *real* Android.

## Verify like a reviewer
```text
[ ] Deny notification permission -> app works, explains the value, no crash
[ ] Token refreshed + stored on launch (no stale-token silence)
[ ] Tap a push -> lands on the SPECIFIC screen (data payload), not generic home
[ ] Android channels exist -> user can mute "tips" but keep "reminders"
[ ] Reminder fires in the user's LOCAL time, not server time
[ ] Tested on real iOS AND real Android hardware (not just simulators)
```

```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Hydra v0.7: push notifications (token lifecycle, targeted sends, channels, deep-link)"
git push
```

You've built push *the right way*, relevant, sparing, user-controlled, and native on both platforms, which is the difference between a re-engagement asset and a one-tap uninstall. Next week: **native modules**, the bridge to device capabilities JavaScript can't reach on its own, and a look under React Native's hood.

weeks.title: Native Modules, When JavaScript Isn't Enough
weeks.context:
React Native runs JavaScript, but most device capabilities (camera, Bluetooth, NFC, advanced sensors) are implemented in native code. Native modules are the bridge between JavaScript and native APIs, they expose native functionality as JavaScript functions. Most of the time, you use pre-built native modules from the Expo SDK or the React Native community. Sometimes, you need to write one yourself.

The old native module API required writing separate implementations in Objective-C/Swift (iOS) and Java/Kotlin (Android), then writing a JavaScript wrapper. The new React Native Architecture uses JSI (JavaScript Interface), native modules register C++ functions that can be called directly from JavaScript without the asynchronous bridge. This is faster and synchronous.

Expo Modules API is the recommended way to write native modules for Expo projects. It provides a TypeScript-first API that generates the boilerplate and handles the bridge. You write the native code (Swift/Kotlin) and the TypeScript interface; Expo Modules handles the wiring. An Expo module is a local package in your project, not a separate npm package.

When you do NOT need a custom native module: most hardware interactions are covered by Expo SDKs. Before writing native code, search the Expo SDK, the React Native community packages, and expo.dev/packages. Expo's managed APIs cover: camera, location, sensors, notifications, secure storage, biometrics, haptics, audio, video, network, brightness, and many more.

When you DO need a custom native module: you need a third-party SDK that only provides a native library (a Bluetooth hardware SDK, a proprietary payment terminal SDK, a specific enterprise MDM integration). Or you need to squeeze performance out of a computation that is too slow in JavaScript. Or you need synchronous access to a native API that only supports async in the available modules.

This week: you write a small Expo Module that exposes the native device battery API, not because you need it (expo-battery covers this), but to understand the pattern. Then you integrate an existing native library.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Native modules: the bridge to everything JavaScript can't reach
React Native runs your app in *JavaScript*, but the device's real powers, the camera, Bluetooth, NFC, advanced sensors, secure enclave, live in *native* code (Swift/Objective-C on iOS, Kotlin/Java on Android). **Native modules** are the *bridge*: they expose native capabilities as JavaScript functions you can call. This week you learn how that bridge works, *when* you need to build one, and how RN's *new architecture* changed the bridge entirely.

## The reassuring truth first
*Most of the time, you do NOT write native modules.* The Expo SDK and the React Native community have already wrapped almost everything, expo-camera, expo-location, expo-notifications, all the modules you've been using *are* native modules someone else wrote. So the honest framing for this week:
```text
99% of the time:  use an EXISTING native module (Expo SDK / community).
Rarely:           you need a capability nobody has wrapped -> write your own.
Always useful:    UNDERSTANDING how the bridge works, so you can debug, evaluate,
                  and reason about performance even when using others' modules.
```
The goal this week is *literacy* more than authorship, you'll write a small module, but the lasting value is understanding the machinery under every package you install.

## What a native module actually is
A native module is *native code* that registers itself with React Native and exposes methods (and constants/events) to JavaScript:
```text
JS side:    NativeModules.MyBattery.getLevel()  // looks like a normal async call
                          |  (crosses the bridge)
Native side: a Swift/Kotlin function reads the actual battery hardware and returns a value
```
The *shape* is always: JS calls a function -> the call crosses into native -> native does the real work (talks to hardware/OS) -> a value comes back to JS, usually *asynchronously*, because crossing into native and back isn't free.

## This week's arc
You'll see *why* and *when* native modules are needed (D2), write one the *old* way and on *Android* (D3-D4), understand the *new architecture* (JSI/TurboModules/Fabric) that replaced the old bridge (D5), and *publish* one as an npm package (D6).

Today, orient: set up the *Expo Modules* tooling (D0) and write down *one* capability Hydra might plausibly need that *isn't* already wrapped by Expo, that's the kind of gap a custom native module fills. Even if you never ship it, naming the gap clarifies when this skill matters.

items.title: Why native modules
items.body:
## Why native modules: the gaps only native code can fill
Before writing a native module, you must recognise *when* you genuinely need one, because building native code adds real cost (two platforms, a development build, more maintenance), and reaching for it unnecessarily is a classic over-engineering trap. Today is about *judgment*: the legitimate reasons, and the cheaper alternatives to rule out first.

## The legitimate reasons to go native
```text
1. A device capability with NO JS wrapper - a niche sensor, a specific Bluetooth/NFC
   protocol, a hardware SDK (a payment terminal, a medical device).
2. A vendor SDK that's native-only - many third-party SDKs (some analytics, some
   hardware vendors) ship as native libraries you must bridge.
3. Performance-critical native work - heavy image/audio/crypto processing that would
   be too slow shuttled through JS.
4. Platform APIs Expo hasn't wrapped - a brand-new iOS/Android API.
```
The common thread: *the capability lives in native land and no one has bridged it for you.* That's the real signal.

## Rule out the cheaper paths FIRST
Most "I need a native module" instincts dissolve under questioning:
```text
- Is there an Expo SDK module?            -> use it.
- Is there a community RN package?         -> use it (vet maintenance/quality).
- Can a backend do this instead?           -> often yes (heavy compute, integrations).
- Can a config plugin tweak native config  -> for native CONFIG (permissions, Info.plist),
  without custom code?                        an Expo config plugin, not a module.
```
*Writing native code is the last resort, not the first move.* A community package, even an imperfect one, is usually cheaper than maintaining your own Swift *and* Kotlin implementations forever.

## The cost you're signing up for
A custom native module means: you maintain *two* native codebases (iOS + Android), you need a *development build* (it won't run in Expo Go), you handle native build issues, and you own it across OS updates. That's a real, ongoing tax, *worth it* for a genuine capability gap, *wasteful* for something a package or backend already solves.

Today: take the capability gap you named yesterday and *interrogate* it against the checklist, is there really no Expo/community module? could a backend do it? Write the honest conclusion. Learning to *talk yourself out of* unnecessary native code is as valuable as learning to write it.

items.title: Old-style React Native modules
items.body:
## Writing a native module: the iOS side (Expo Modules)
Today you write a *real* (if tiny) native module so the bridge stops being abstract. The modern, far-easier way is the **Expo Modules API**, which lets you write clean Swift (iOS) and Kotlin (Android) with a declarative DSL, *vastly* simpler than the old Objective-C/Java boilerplate. We'll build a trivial example, a module that returns the device's battery level, to see the whole round-trip.

## The Expo Modules definition (iOS, Swift)
With `npx create-expo-module`, you get a module scaffold. The iOS implementation is a *definition* block:
```swift
import ExpoModulesCore
import UIKit

public class BatteryModule: Module {
  public func definition() -> ModuleDefinition {
    Name("Battery")                       // the JS-visible name

    Function("getLevel") {                 // a sync function exposed to JS
      UIDevice.current.isBatteryMonitoringEnabled = true
      return UIDevice.current.batteryLevel  // reads the real hardware
    }
  }
}
```
That's it, *no manual bridging headers, no RCT_EXPORT macros*. `Name`, `Function`, `AsyncFunction`, `Events`, `Constants` are the building blocks. The Expo Modules API generates the JS<->native plumbing for you.

## Calling it from JavaScript
```tsx
import Battery from './modules/battery';
const level = Battery.getLevel();   // 0.0 .. 1.0 (or -1 on simulator)
```
From JS it looks like any function, *the native code runs the moment you call it.* `AsyncFunction` (instead of `Function`) is used for anything that does real work (I/O, hardware that's slow), returning a Promise, *the same async pattern you've seen in every Expo API.*

## Why the old way matters too (tomorrow)
The Expo Modules API is the *modern* path and what you should use. But you'll still encounter the *old-style* React Native module API (`RCT_EXPORT_MODULE`, `NativeModules`) in older libraries and docs, so tomorrow you'll see the Android side and understand the legacy approach, which makes you able to read and fix *any* native module you meet, not just ones built the new way.

## The dev-build reality
A custom native module *cannot run in Expo Go*, Expo Go only contains the modules Expo pre-bundled. You need a **development build** (`eas build --profile development`) that includes *your* native code. This is the moment many developers first leave Expo Go, and W21's EAS Build is where that becomes routine.

Today: scaffold a tiny Expo module (battery level, or device uptime) with an iOS Swift `Function`, call it from JS in a dev build, and see your *own* native code return a real hardware value. The bridge is no longer a mystery.

items.title: Android
items.body:
## The Android side: Kotlin, and the cross-platform contract
A native module isn't done until it works on *both* platforms. Today you implement the *Android* (Kotlin) side of yesterday's module and confront the central challenge of native modules: *you're maintaining two implementations that must present one identical JavaScript API.*

## The Android implementation (Kotlin, Expo Modules)
The Expo Modules API uses the *same* declarative DSL on Android, so the structure mirrors iOS:
```kotlin
import expo.modules.kotlin.modules.Module
import expo.modules.kotlin.modules.ModuleDefinition

class BatteryModule : Module() {
  override fun definition() = ModuleDefinition {
    Name("Battery")                          // SAME name as iOS

    Function("getLevel") {                    // SAME function name & contract
      val bm = appContext.reactContext
        ?.getSystemService(Context.BATTERY_SERVICE) as BatteryManager
      bm.getIntProperty(BatteryManager.BATTERY_PROPERTY_CAPACITY) / 100.0
    }
  }
}
```
The *JS-facing contract* (`Name("Battery")`, `getLevel` returning 0..1) is *identical* to iOS, but the *implementation* uses Android's `BatteryManager` instead of iOS's `UIDevice`. *This is the essence of a native module:* one JS API, two native realisations.

## The hard part: keeping the two in sync
The discipline that makes native modules maintainable:
```text
- IDENTICAL JS API on both platforms (same names, same argument shapes,
  same return types) - or you've built two different modules wearing one name.
- Consistent BEHAVIOUR - getLevel should mean the same thing on both, including
  edge cases (what does it return when unknown? -1 on both, not -1 vs null).
- Platform DIFFERENCES handled gracefully - if a capability exists on one platform
  only, document it and degrade predictably (return null / throw a clear error),
  never crash.
```
*A native module with subtly different behaviour per platform is a bug factory*, the JS developer calling it (often you, later) assumes one contract and gets surprised on one OS.

## Test on both, always
Native code behaves differently across OS versions and devices far more than JS does. *Run your module on a real iPhone AND a real Android*, and on a couple of OS versions if you can. The battery example even differs on simulators (iOS sim returns -1). *"Works on iOS" is half a test.*

Today: implement the Android (Kotlin) side of your module so the *same* JS call works on both platforms with the *same* contract, and verify on real Android hardware. Holding one identical API across two native codebases is the core craft, and the main cost, of native modules.

days.title: Bridge architecture (old) vs JSI / TurboModules / Fabric (new)
days.summary: Focus: Bridge architecture (old) vs JSI / TurboModules / Fabric (new)

items.title: Bridge architecture (old) vs JSI / TurboModules / Fabric (new)
items.body:
## The bridge, old vs new: JSI, TurboModules, Fabric
To truly understand React Native, and why the *new architecture* exists, you need to know how JavaScript and native code *communicate*. The mechanism changed fundamentally: the old **bridge** has been replaced by **JSI / TurboModules / Fabric**. This isn't trivia; it explains performance characteristics, async patterns, and where RN is heading.

## The old architecture: the asynchronous bridge
Originally, JS and native were *separate worlds* connected by a **bridge** that passed *serialised JSON messages*:
```text
JS thread  --(serialize to JSON)-->  bridge  --(deserialize)-->  Native thread
```
Three consequences defined old RN: communication was **asynchronous** (you couldn't get a native value *synchronously*), **batched** (messages queued and sent together), and **serialised** (everything became JSON strings, a real cost for large/ frequent data). This is *why* so many RN APIs are Promise-based and why passing big data or doing per-frame native work was painful, *every crossing paid the serialisation tax.*

## The new architecture: JSI removes the wall
**JSI (JavaScript Interface)** lets JavaScript hold *direct references* to native objects and call them *synchronously*, no JSON, no batching, no separate-worlds wall. Built on JSI:
```text
- TurboModules: the new native MODULES - lazy-loaded (only loaded when used),
  can be called SYNCHRONOUSLY, no serialisation. Faster startup, faster calls.
- Fabric: the new rendering system (the UI layer) - lets native UI and JS stay in
  sync more efficiently, enabling smoother, more concurrent rendering.
- Codegen: generates the type-safe glue between JS and native from typed specs.
```
The upshot: *less overhead, synchronous capability when appropriate, better performance, and the foundation for modern concurrent React.*

## Why this matters to you, practically
```text
- Modern Expo / RN apps run on the NEW architecture by default - you're already on it.
- The Expo Modules API you used (D3-D4) builds TurboModules under the hood - you got
  the new architecture "for free" without writing low-level JSI.
- It explains performance: old bridge = serialisation cost; new = direct calls.
- When evaluating old libraries, "is it new-architecture compatible?" is now a real
  question - some unmaintained packages still assume the old bridge.
```
You rarely touch JSI directly, but understanding it is what lets you reason about performance and compatibility instead of treating RN as magic.

Today: confirm your project is on the new architecture, and write a short note in your own words explaining the *old bridge* (async, batched, serialised) vs *JSI/TurboModules/Fabric* (direct, sync-capable, faster), and one *practical* implication for app performance. Being able to explain this is a senior-level RN literacy marker.

items.title: Publishing a native module as an npm package
items.body:
## Publishing a native module as an npm package
A native module becomes truly valuable when it's *reusable*, packaged so you (and others) can `npm install` it into any project. Today you learn to *publish* an Expo native module as an npm package, which is also how the entire RN ecosystem you depend on is built. Even if you never publish publicly, this is how you share modules across your own apps and contribute back.

## What a publishable module contains
`create-expo-module` scaffolds the right structure:
```text
my-module/
  src/            - the JS/TS API + types (what consumers import)
  ios/            - Swift implementation
  android/        - Kotlin implementation
  expo-module.config.json - tells Expo how to wire the native code
  package.json    - name, version, peerDependencies (expo, react-native)
  example/        - a runnable example app (also your dev/test harness)
```
The *example app* matters more than it looks, it's both your *test bed* and the *proof* to consumers that the module works. A module without a working example is a module nobody trusts.

## Publishing the package
```bash
# 1) Build the JS, lint, and TEST in the example app (on BOTH platforms)
# 2) Set a sensible semver version in package.json
npm version 1.0.0
# 3) Publish to npm
npm publish --access public
```
Consumers then `npx expo install your-module`, and because it ships native code, they need a *development build* (Expo Go can't load arbitrary native code, the recurring constraint).

## What makes a module *good* (and used)
```text
- A clear, typed JS API (TypeScript types are non-negotiable now).
- BOTH platforms implemented with an identical contract (W12 D4).
- New-architecture compatible (TurboModule), the Expo Modules API gives you this.
- A README: what it does, install, usage, platform support, permissions needed.
- Honest platform-support notes (iOS-only? Android 8+? say so).
- Semantic versioning + a changelog, so consumers can upgrade safely.
```
*This is the same professionalism bar as any open-source package*, the difference between a module people adopt and one they avoid is documentation, types, and reliability, not cleverness.

## The ecosystem view
Every Expo SDK and community module you've used was published exactly this way. Understanding the publishing flow demystifies your *dependencies*, you can now read a module's source, evaluate its quality, fix a bug and PR it, or fork it if it's abandoned. *You've gone from consumer to potential contributor.*

Today: take your battery (or chosen) module, give it a typed JS API, a real README with platform-support notes, and a working example app, then either publish it to npm or do a full `npm pack` dry-run. Packaging native code to a professional standard is what turns a one-off into a reusable asset.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: a published (or package-ready) native module
Package the week into a *real native module*, written for both platforms, new-architecture compatible, documented, and either published to npm or fully package-ready. This proves you understand React Native *to its foundations*, not just as a JS framework, but as a JS-native bridge you can extend.

## What to ship
- A **working Expo native module** exposing a genuine native capability, with **iOS (Swift)** and **Android (Kotlin)** implementations behind an **identical, typed JS API**.
- Running in a **development build** on *both* real platforms (it can't run in Expo Go, and that's expected).
- A **README** (purpose, install, usage, platform support, any permissions), a **typed API**, and a **working example app**.
- **Published to npm** (or a clean `npm pack` dry-run if you'd rather not publish publicly).

## Verify like a maintainer
```text
[ ] Same JS API works identically on real iOS AND real Android
[ ] Edge cases consistent across platforms (unknown value -> same result, no crash)
[ ] New-architecture / TurboModule compatible (Expo Modules API gives this)
[ ] README states platform support honestly; types ship with the package
[ ] Example app runs and demonstrates it
```

```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Native module: cross-platform Expo module (Swift + Kotlin, typed JS API, published)"
git push
```

You now understand the bridge that *every* React Native capability crosses, you've written native code on both platforms, held one API across two implementations, grasped the JSI/TurboModule architecture, and packaged it like the libraries you depend on. That foundational literacy makes you able to *debug, evaluate, and extend* any part of the RN stack. Next week we come back up to JavaScript for **networking, APIs, offline, and sync**, the reality that mobile apps live on flaky connections and must work anyway.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: What is the React Native bridge and what are its performance limitations? The bridge is a serialised, asynchronous, batched channel between JavaScript and native code. Every native call is serialised to JSON, sent across the bridge, deserialised, executed, the result serialised and sent back. This round trip takes microseconds in the best case but the serialisation overhead means you cannot call native functions thousands of times per second. The bridge is also asynchronous, you cannot synchronously read a native value and use it in the same JavaScript expression. JSI (the new architecture) replaces the bridge with direct C++ function calls, synchronous, faster, no serialisation.

weeks.title: Networking, APIs, Offline, Sync
weeks.context:
Mobile apps live on unreliable networks. Cellular connections drop in tunnels. Users switch between Wi-Fi and 4G. A user in a rural area might have 2G for an hour. Your app must degrade gracefully when the network is unavailable and catch up when it returns. An app that shows a blank screen when offline is not a production app.

Network state detection: expo-network provides NetInfo.fetch() and NetInfo.addEventListener for network state changes. But detecting "connected to Wi-Fi" does not mean the internet is actually reachable, the user might be connected to a hotel Wi-Fi with a captive portal. A real connectivity check pings a known server.

Optimistic updates: when the user takes an action (checks off a habit, sends a message), update the UI immediately without waiting for the server response. Then send the network request in the background. If it fails, roll back the UI change and show an error. This makes the app feel instant even on slow networks.

Request queuing: for actions taken offline (the user adds a habit while on a plane), queue the request and execute it when connectivity returns. expo-task-manager with a background fetch can process the queue when the app is in the background.

Caching API responses: for data that does not change frequently (menu items, user profile), cache the last successful response locally. When the app loads, show the cached data immediately while fetching fresh data in the background. This is the stale-while-revalidate pattern, the app never shows a blank loading state.

react-query (also called TanStack Query) is the standard library for server state management in React Native. It handles: caching, background refetching, deduplication (multiple components requesting the same data get one request), optimistic updates, error boundaries, and offline support. It replaces most of the custom networking code you would otherwise write.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Mobile networking: build for the network you don't control
This week is **networking**, and the mobile premise reframes everything you know from the web: *the network is unreliable by default.* Connections drop in tunnels and lifts, users switch Wi-Fi to 4G mid-action, a rural user crawls on 2G. *An app that shows a blank screen when offline is not a production app.* So the week's goal is bigger than "call an API", it's building apps that *degrade gracefully offline and catch up when the network returns.*

## The mobile-network realities
```text
- Connections DROP constantly (tunnels, lifts, dead zones, switching networks).
- "Connected to Wi-Fi" != "has working internet" (captive portals, no backhaul).
- Latency and bandwidth VARY wildly (fibre Wi-Fi vs congested 2G).
- Requests get INTERRUPTED mid-flight - partial failures are normal, not rare.
- Battery + data are FINITE - chatty apps drain both and annoy users on metered plans.
```
Designing for this isn't pessimism, it's *realism*. The best mobile apps *feel* fast and reliable on bad networks precisely because they were *built* for bad networks.

## The strategy: cache-first, sync-later
The mental model that solves most of it:
```text
1. Show CACHED data instantly (the app is never blank, even offline).
2. Fetch fresh data in the background; update the UI when it arrives.
3. Queue user ACTIONS made offline; replay them when connectivity returns.
```
This is the difference between an app that's a *thin window onto a server* (useless offline) and one that's *locally resilient with the server as a sync target* (works anywhere). You already have the storage skills (W8) to cache; this week adds the *networking and sync* layer on top.

## This week's toolkit
You'll use **TanStack Query** (server-state with caching/retries/background refetch baked in), **expo-network / NetInfo** (network-state detection), an *offline action queue* (background sync), token-aware requests (auth), and API *versioning* awareness. Hydra becomes an app that logs water *offline at the gym* and syncs when you're back on Wi-Fi.

Today, orient: install `axios` and `@tanstack/react-query`, wrap the app in a `QueryClientProvider`, and make *one* cached GET request. Then airplane-mode the device and confirm the *cached* data still shows. Seeing the app *not* go blank offline is the week's whole thesis in miniature.

items.title: TanStack Query on RN
items.body:
## TanStack Query: server state that handles the hard parts for you
Naive data fetching, `useEffect` + `fetch` + `useState` loading/error flags, falls apart on mobile: no caching, no retries, no background refresh, manual everything, and it re-fetches on every mount. **TanStack Query** (React Query) is the standard solution: it treats *server data as a cache you keep in sync*, and it handles caching, retries, deduplication, and background refetching *for you*. On a flaky mobile network, this is transformative.

## The core hook
```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

const { data, isLoading, error, refetch } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ['logs', userId],            // the cache identity
  queryFn: () => api.get(`/logs?u=${userId}`).then(r => r.data),
  staleTime: 60_000,                      // treat data fresh for 60s (don't refetch)
});
```
That one hook gives you: a *cache* keyed by `queryKey` (so the data is instantly available on the next mount, no blank screen), automatic *loading/error* state, *retries* on failure, *deduplication* (two components asking for the same key = one request), and *background refetch* (show cached data, quietly fetch fresh).

## Why it's a mobile superpower
```text
- Cache-first rendering -> the app shows data INSTANTLY, even offline (W13's thesis).
- Automatic retries -> transient mobile failures recover without your code.
- staleTime / gcTime -> YOU tune how aggressively to refetch vs save data/battery.
- refetchOnReconnect -> when the network returns, it refreshes automatically.
- Pairs with persistence -> cache can be saved to disk (AsyncStorage/MMKV) so data
  survives app restarts, true offline reads.
```
That last point is key on mobile: with the *persistence* plugin, TanStack Query writes its cache to storage, so a user who opens your app *offline* still sees their last-known data. The server becomes a *sync target*, not a *requirement*.

## Mutations (changing data)
For writes, `useMutation` handles the action plus cache updates, and supports **optimistic updates** (update the UI immediately, before the server confirms), which is what makes mobile apps *feel* instant:
```tsx
const add = useMutation({
  mutationFn: (log) => api.post('/logs', log),
  onMutate: async (log) => { /* optimistically add to the cache now */ },
  onError: (_e,_v,ctx) => { /* roll back if it fails */ },
});
```
Optimistic updates are the foundation of the offline-write experience you'll build this week.

Today: convert one of Hydra's data screens to TanStack Query with a persisted cache, then airplane-mode the app and confirm it *still renders* the cached logs and recovers automatically on reconnect. You've just made your data layer resilient instead of fragile.

items.title: Background sync
items.body:
## Background sync: queue offline actions, replay them later
This is the feature that makes an app *truly* offline-capable: the user *acts* while offline, logs water at the gym with no signal, and the app *accepts it locally* and *syncs it to the server when connectivity returns.* This **offline action queue** (a form of background sync) is what separates a real mobile app from a thin server window.

## The pattern: local-first writes with a sync queue
```text
1. User acts offline -> WRITE to local storage immediately (W8: SQLite/MMKV),
   mark it 'pending', update the UI optimistically (it looks done).
2. Add the action to a SYNC QUEUE (a list of pending operations).
3. When online (W13 D3 detects it) -> process the queue: send each pending action
   to the server, and on success mark it 'synced' (or remove it).
4. Handle conflicts + failures (below).
```
The user *never* waits for the network and *never* loses an action. The app feels instant and works in a tunnel; the sync is invisible plumbing.

## The realities you must handle
```text
- IDEMPOTENCY: a queued action might send TWICE (retry after a flaky success).
  Give each a client-generated ID so the server can dedupe -> no double-logged water.
- ORDERING: replay actions in the order they happened (or your server state is wrong).
- CONFLICTS: the same record changed on two devices while offline. Pick a strategy:
  last-write-wins (simple), server-wins, or merge (complex). Decide DELIBERATELY.
- PARTIAL FAILURE: action 3 of 10 fails -> don't lose 4-10; keep them queued, retry
  with backoff, and surface persistent failures to the user.
- FEEDBACK: show per-item status (pending / synced / failed) so the user trusts it.
```
*Idempotency and conflict strategy are the hard parts*, naive sync double-creates records and silently overwrites data. A client-generated ID + a chosen conflict policy prevents the worst of it.

## Where the tools fit
TanStack Query's *mutations* with **optimistic updates** (D2) give you the instant-UI half; persisting the queue (SQLite/MMKV) gives durability across restarts; network detection (D3) triggers the flush. Libraries like *TanStack Query's persistence* or dedicated offline-sync layers (WatermelonDB, PowerSync, Replicache) productise this for complex cases, but understanding the *manual* pattern first is what lets you use them wisely.

Today: implement an offline log queue for Hydra, logging while in airplane mode writes locally + queues (UI shows it as pending), and turning the network back on flushes the queue to the server (idempotently, with per-item status). Watch a tunnel-logged glass of water appear on the server when you reconnect. That's real offline capability.

items.title: API versioning
items.body:
## API versioning: surviving the fact that old app versions live forever
Here's a reality that has no web equivalent: *you cannot force users to update.* When you ship a web app, everyone's on the new version instantly. On mobile, a user on v1.0 coexists with users on v1.2 and v1.5 *for months or years*, and your backend must serve them *all*. **API versioning** is how you evolve your API without breaking the old app versions still in the wild. Understanding this shapes how you design every endpoint.

## The core problem
```text
Web:    deploy -> 100% of users on new version immediately.
Mobile: ship v2 -> users TRICKLE to it over weeks; many NEVER update.
        Your backend simultaneously serves v1.0, v1.1, v1.2... live, in production.
```
So a "small breaking change" to an API response, renaming a field, removing one, changing a type, *crashes every old app version still installed.* That's an outage you can't fix by redeploying, because the broken code is on users' phones.

## Versioning strategies
```text
- URL versioning:    /v1/logs, /v2/logs   (explicit, common, easy to reason about)
- Header versioning: Accept: application/vnd.app.v2+json
- The golden rule:   ADDITIVE changes are safe; BREAKING changes need a new version.
```
*Additive* (adding a new optional field, a new endpoint) doesn't break old clients, they ignore what they don't know. *Breaking* (removing/renaming a field, changing types/semantics) requires a new version so old clients keep hitting the old contract.

## Designing the client to be resilient
Your *app* should also be defensive, because it'll meet API changes too:
```text
- Tolerate UNKNOWN/extra fields (don't crash on a field you didn't expect).
- Handle MISSING optional fields gracefully (default them).
- VALIDATE/parse responses (e.g. with zod) so a malformed payload fails safely,
  not with a cryptic crash deep in the UI.
- Send the app version in requests so the backend can adapt or warn.
```

## Force-update as the escape hatch
Sometimes you *must* drop support for very old versions (a security fix, a hard breaking change). Then you need a **force-update** mechanism: the app checks a "minimum supported version" from the server and, if too old, blocks with a "please update" screen. You'll build this properly in **W22 (updates/OTA)**; for now, know it's the deliberate, last-resort way to retire old clients, and that *good versioning minimises how often you need it.*

Today: version Hydra's API thinking, define `/v1` endpoints, write down which kinds of changes are *additive-safe* vs *breaking*, and make the client *tolerant* of unknown/missing fields (parse responses defensively). Then sketch a minimum-version check. Designing for "old versions live forever" is a mobile mindset shift the web never taught you.

items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: Hydra v0.8, offline-capable and resilient
Package the week into **Hydra v0.8**: an app that *works on bad networks*, instant cached reads, offline writes that sync later, resilient authenticated requests, and version-tolerant API handling. This is the difference between a demo that needs perfect Wi-Fi and a *real* mobile app.

## What v0.8 must demonstrate
- **Cache-first data (TanStack Query):** screens render *instantly* from a *persisted* cache, never blank, even offline; stale data refetches in the background and on reconnect.
- **True network awareness:** behaviour driven by `isInternetReachable` (not just `isConnected`), with an honest offline/syncing indicator, debounced against flapping.
- **Offline action queue:** logging while offline writes locally + queues; reconnecting flushes the queue *idempotently* (client-generated IDs, no double-logs), with per-item pending/synced/failed status.
- **Resilient auth:** an interceptor attaches the token; a *single-flight* 401-refresh transparently renews and replays requests.
- **Version tolerance:** the client parses responses defensively (unknown/missing fields don't crash).

## Verify like a reviewer (the test is the network)
```text
[ ] Airplane mode on launch -> app shows cached data, not a blank/error screen
[ ] Log water offline -> appears immediately (pending); syncs on reconnect ONCE
[ ] Captive-portal/flaky Wi-Fi -> app trusts reachability, doesn't hang firing requests
[ ] Several requests with an expired token -> ONE refresh, all succeed (no logout loop)
[ ] Feed it a response with an extra/missing field -> no crash
```

```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Hydra v0.8: offline-capable (cache-first, sync queue, token refresh, version-tolerant)"
git push
```

You've built for the network you *don't* control, which is the defining discipline of mobile networking. Hydra now logs water in a tunnel and catches up on Wi-Fi, exactly what users expect and most apps fail to do. Next week: **authentication on mobile**, the full picture, biometrics (Face ID/Touch ID), OAuth in an in-app browser, secure token storage, and staying logged in for months.

weeks.title: Authentication on Mobile, OAuth, Biometrics, Sessions
weeks.context:
Authentication on mobile has unique challenges compared to the web. There is no browser cookie jar. Sessions must be stored securely. The user expects to stay logged in for weeks or months without being asked to re-authenticate. And mobile adds capabilities the web does not have: biometric authentication (Face ID, Touch ID, fingerprint) as a convenient and secure unlock mechanism.

Token storage: after a successful login, you receive an access token (short-lived, e.g., 15 minutes) and a refresh token (long-lived, e.g., 30 days). Store both in expo-secure-store (iOS Keychain, Android Keystore). Never store them in AsyncStorage or MMKV (plaintext). The access token goes in the Authorization header of every API request. The refresh token is used to get a new access token when the current one expires.

Axios interceptors: configure an Axios instance with a request interceptor that adds the Authorization header, and a response interceptor that detects 401 responses, refreshes the token, and retries the original request. The user never knows the token was refreshed, they stay logged in transparently.

OAuth on mobile uses the device browser (not a WebView) for the OAuth flow. This is a security requirement, WebViews allow the app to read the credentials the user enters, defeating the purpose of OAuth. expo-auth-session handles this: it opens the system browser for the OAuth flow and uses a deep link to return the authorization code to your app. Configure your app's URL scheme in app.json.

Biometric authentication is not a replacement for your primary auth, it is a local unlock mechanism. The user's credentials (password or token) live in secure storage. When they open the app, instead of showing a login screen, you show a "Unlock with Face ID" prompt. If they authenticate with biometrics, you read the token from secure storage and use it. If biometrics fail or are unavailable, fall back to password.

Session management: decide when the user should be logged out. Options: never log out (refresh token rotates on use, revoke on explicit logout), log out after N days of inactivity (track lastActiveAt), log out when the app is uninstalled (secure store persists across reinstalls on iOS unless you clear it, decide whether you want this behaviour).

concept_check.q: A user's access token expires while they are in the middle of using the app. How does the Axios interceptor handle this transparently? The interceptor catches the 401 response. It calls the refresh to?

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Authentication on mobile: different rules than the web
This week is **authentication**, and the mobile context changes the rules you learned on the web. *There is no browser cookie jar.* Sessions must be stored *securely* on the device. The user expects to stay logged in for *weeks or months* without re-entering a password. And mobile adds a capability the web doesn't have: **biometrics**, Face ID, Touch ID, fingerprint, as a fast, secure unlock. Getting auth right is non-negotiable: it's the front door, and a weak one is a breach.

## What makes mobile auth distinct
```text
- No cookies -> you manage TOKENS yourself (access + refresh), in SECURE storage.
- Long-lived sessions -> users expect "stay logged in" for months (refresh tokens).
- Biometrics -> Face ID/Touch ID/fingerprint as a convenient, secure local unlock.
- OAuth in an in-app browser -> "Sign in with Google/Apple" via a secure web flow.
- Deep links -> email confirmations / magic links must open the APP, not a browser.
- Secure storage -> tokens live in the Keychain (iOS) / Keystore (Android), never plain.
```
Each of these is a thing the web either handled for you (cookies) or simply couldn't do (biometrics, deep links into an app). This week covers them all.

## The token model (recap + secure-storage twist)
You met the *networking* side of tokens in W13. The *security* side:
```text
- ACCESS token  - short-lived (~15 min), sent on every request.
- REFRESH token - long-lived (weeks), used ONLY to mint new access tokens.
- BOTH live in SECURE storage (expo-secure-store -> Keychain/Keystore),
  NEVER in AsyncStorage (which is plaintext on disk and readable on a rooted device).
```
*Storing a token in AsyncStorage is a real, common security bug.* Tokens are credentials; they belong in the hardware-backed secure store.

## Biometrics: convenience that's also security
Face ID/Touch ID let a user *re-authenticate* with a glance instead of a password, the OS verifies them locally and your app unlocks (e.g. reveals a stored session, or gates a sensitive screen). It's *both* better UX *and* better security than typing a password people reuse. You'll wire it with `expo-local-authentication`.

Today, orient: install `expo-secure-store` and `expo-local-authentication`, store a dummy token in the secure store (not AsyncStorage), and read it back. Then write down Hydra's intended auth: which sign-in methods, and where biometrics would gate access. Designing the auth model before coding it is what prevents security holes later.

items.title: Auth flows on mobile
items.body:
## Auth flows on mobile: choosing how users sign in
There are several ways a mobile app can authenticate a user, and choosing the right *mix* shapes security, UX, and how much you build. Today you map the flows and pick Hydra's.

## The main flows
```text
- Email + password    - classic; you store the hash server-side, manage reset flows.
- Magic link / OTP     - passwordless: email a link or SMS a code. No password to leak,
                         but needs deep-linking (D5) or code entry.
- Social / OAuth       - "Sign in with Google/Apple/GitHub". Fast, no password for you to
                         store; uses an in-app browser flow (D4). Apple sign-in is often
                         REQUIRED by App Store if you offer other social logins.
- Biometric unlock     - not a sign-in METHOD per se, but a fast re-auth gate over an
                         existing session (Face ID to reopen the app).
```
Most production apps offer *two or three*: email/password *or* social, plus biometric re-unlock. *More options = more to build and maintain*, so choose deliberately for your audience.

## The "stay logged in" expectation
The defining mobile UX: *users log in once and stay logged in for months.* You achieve this with the token model, after first login, you securely store the *refresh* token, and on each app launch you silently mint a fresh *access* token from it. The user only sees a login screen again if the refresh token *expires or is revoked*. *Asking a mobile user to log in every session is a UX failure*, the web habit of short sessions doesn't transfer.

## Biometric gate over a stored session
A common, elegant pattern combines long sessions with security:
```text
1. User logs in once -> store refresh token in SECURE store.
2. On reopen -> require Face ID/Touch ID (expo-local-authentication) to UNLOCK.
3. On success -> use the stored refresh token to resume the session silently.
```
```tsx
import * as LocalAuthentication from 'expo-local-authentication';
const ok = await LocalAuthentication.authenticateAsync({
  promptMessage: 'Unlock Hydra',
});
if (ok.success) resumeSession();
```
This gives "stay logged in for months" *and* "but a glance is required to open it", the best of both, and what users of banking/health apps expect.

## The App Store rule worth knowing now
If you offer *any* third-party social login (Google, Facebook), Apple generally *requires* you to also offer **Sign in with Apple**. Plan for it if social login is in scope, discovering it at submission (W24) is a painful surprise.

Today: implement Hydra's chosen sign-in (start with email/password *or* one social provider) plus a *biometric unlock* over the stored session. Confirm the user logs in once, closes the app, reopens, and unlocks with Face ID/fingerprint without re-typing a password. That flow *is* modern mobile auth.

items.title: Think it through
items.body: Store an auth token in AsyncStorage. Now in expo-secure-store. What's the security difference?

items.title: Refresh tokens
items.body:
## Refresh tokens: staying logged in, securely
The mechanism that delivers "logged in for months" *without* compromising security is the **access + refresh token** pair. You met the *request-retry* side in W13; today is the *lifecycle and security* side, how to store, rotate, and revoke these credentials safely on a device.

## Why two tokens (the security logic)
```text
ACCESS token  - SHORT life (~15 min). Sent on every request. If stolen, it's useless
                in minutes. This short life is WHY it's safe to send constantly.
REFRESH token - LONG life (weeks/months). Sent ONLY to the refresh endpoint to mint
                new access tokens. It is the crown jewel -> guard it hardest.
```
The split *limits blast radius*: a leaked access token expires fast; the powerful refresh token is rarely transmitted and lives only in secure storage. *One long-lived token used everywhere would be both a UX win and a security disaster*, the pair gives you the UX *and* the safety.

## Storing them right
```tsx
import * as SecureStore from 'expo-secure-store';
await SecureStore.setItemAsync('refresh', refreshToken); // Keychain/Keystore, encrypted
const t = await SecureStore.getItemAsync('refresh');
```
*Always* secure-store for tokens, hardware-backed, encrypted, and protected from other apps. Optionally require biometrics to *read* the most sensitive items (`requireAuthentication`). *Never* log tokens, never put them in a push payload, never store them in AsyncStorage.

## Refresh-token rotation (the modern, safer pattern)
Best practice is **rotation**: every time you use a refresh token, the server issues a *new* refresh token and invalidates the old one. The payoff:
```text
- A stolen refresh token works only until the legit app refreshes next, then it's dead.
- If a rotated (already-used) token reappears -> the server detects THEFT and can
  revoke the whole session family. This is "refresh token reuse detection".
```
Your client just stores whatever new refresh token comes back; the *server* enforces rotation. Knowing it exists lets you build (or expect) a properly secure backend.

## Revocation and logout
Logout must do *two* things: clear tokens from secure storage *and* tell the server to *revoke* the refresh token (so a copy can't be reused). And handle *forced* logout gracefully: if a refresh fails because the token was revoked (password change, "log out all devices"), clear local state and route to login *cleanly*, no crash, no infinite retry (the W13 refresh-loop guard).

Today: implement Hydra's full token lifecycle, secure-store the refresh token, silent access-token mint on launch, and a logout that *both* clears secure storage *and* revokes server-side. Bonus: gate reading the token behind biometrics. Tokens handled this way are what keep users both *logged in* and *safe*.

items.body: OAuth via webview, why is it forbidden by Google's OAuth policies? What can go wrong?

items.title: In-app browser for OAuth
items.body:
## OAuth via the in-app browser: "Sign in with Google" done right
"Sign in with Google/Apple/GitHub" is an **OAuth** flow, and on mobile there's a *right* way and several *wrong, insecure* ways to do it. The right way uses a **secure in-app browser** (`expo-auth-session` + `expo-web-browser`), not a WebView, and not your own login form for someone else's service. Getting this right is both a security and an App Store requirement.

## Why a special browser, not a WebView
```text
WRONG: render Google's login in a WebView you control.
   -> You could read the user's Google password (so Google BLOCKS this), it's phishing-shaped,
      and it doesn't share the system login session.
RIGHT: open the provider in a SECURE system browser tab (ASWebAuthenticationSession on
   iOS / Chrome Custom Tabs on Android), via expo-web-browser.
   -> The provider's REAL login UI, the user's existing session/cookies, and your app
      never touches their password. This is what OAuth providers REQUIRE.
```
*Providers actively reject WebView-based OAuth.* The secure system browser is non-negotiable, and Expo's tools give it to you.

## The flow with expo-auth-session (PKCE)
```tsx
import * as AuthSession from 'expo-auth-session';

const redirectUri = AuthSession.makeRedirectUri({ scheme: 'hydra' }); // your app scheme
const request = new AuthSession.AuthRequest({
  clientId, scopes: ['openid','email'], redirectUri,
  usePKCE: true,                       // PKCE: secure auth for PUBLIC clients (mobile)
});
const result = await request.promptAsync(discovery); // opens the secure browser
// result.params.code -> exchange server-side for tokens
```
Two essentials:
```text
- PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange): mandatory for mobile because apps are "public
  clients" (they can't keep a client SECRET safe). PKCE secures the code exchange
  WITHOUT a client secret. expo-auth-session does PKCE for you (usePKCE: true).
- REDIRECT back to your app: after login, the provider redirects to your app's URL
  scheme / universal link, which reopens your app with an auth code (this is deep
  linking, D5). You exchange that code for tokens (ideally server-side).
```

## Don't put the client secret in the app
A mobile app *cannot* hold a client secret, anyone can decompile the binary and extract it. So the *code-for-token* exchange that needs the secret should happen on *your backend*, or use providers/flows designed for public clients (PKCE, no secret). *A client secret shipped in an app is a leaked secret.*

Today: wire one social login (Google or GitHub) in Hydra using `expo-auth-session` with PKCE, opening the *secure system browser*, and complete the redirect back into the app. Confirm you never render the provider's login in a WebView and never embed a client secret. Secure OAuth is a hard requirement, both providers and Apple enforce it.

items.title: Deep linking from email confirmation
items.body:
## Deep linking: getting email links and redirects back into your app
OAuth redirects (D4), email confirmations, magic links, password resets, and marketing links all share one need: *a URL must open your APP, on the right screen, not a web browser.* That's **deep linking**, and it's foundational mobile plumbing that also powers a lot of growth and onboarding.

## The two kinds of deep link
```text
- CUSTOM SCHEME:    hydra://reset?token=abc
    Simple to set up; works for OAuth redirects and in-app navigation.
    Downside: if the app ISN'T installed, the link just fails (nothing handles it).
- UNIVERSAL LINKS (iOS) / APP LINKS (Android):   https://hydra.app/reset?token=abc
    A REAL https URL that opens the app if installed, else falls back to your website.
    Requires hosting a verification file (apple-app-site-association / assetlinks.json)
    proving you own the domain. More setup, far better UX, and the modern standard.
```
*Custom schemes are fine for OAuth redirects and internal links; universal links are what you want for email/marketing links* (because they degrade gracefully to the web when the app isn't installed).

## Handling links with expo-router / expo-linking
```tsx
import * as Linking from 'expo-linking';

// Cold start: app opened FROM a link
const url = await Linking.getInitialURL();

// Warm: app already running, a link arrives
const sub = Linking.addEventListener('url', ({ url }) => routeFromUrl(url));
```
With **expo-router**, file-based routes map to URLs automatically, an incoming `hydra://logs/42` opens the `app/logs/[id]` screen, so much of the routing is handled for you once the scheme/links are configured. You parse the URL, extract params (the reset token, the log id), and navigate.

## The flows deep linking unlocks
```text
- Email confirmation / magic link -> tap in email -> app opens, verifies the token,
  logs the user in. (Ties directly to passwordless auth, W14 D2.)
- Password reset -> link opens the reset screen with the token.
- OAuth redirect -> provider sends the user back into the app (W14 D4).
- Sharing / growth -> "open this log in Hydra" links that launch the app deep.
```

## The cold-start gotcha
The classic bug: a link works when the app is *already open* (event listener) but does *nothing* on a *cold start* (app was closed). You must handle *both*, `getInitialURL()` for cold starts *and* the event listener for warm. *Test both states*, they're different code paths and the cold-start one is easy to forget.

Today: configure Hydra's URL scheme (and ideally a universal/app link), then handle a *magic-link-style* deep link, tapping `hydra://verify?token=...` opens the app and completes a verification, working from *both* a cold start and while running. Deep linking is the glue that makes email auth and shareable links actually work on mobile.

items.title: Auth providers on mobile
items.body:
## Auth providers on mobile: build vs buy
You can build authentication yourself, or use a *managed auth provider*. For most teams, *buying* auth is the right call: security is hard, high-stakes, and a solved problem, and a good provider handles tokens, social login, MFA, and breaches better than you will. Today is the *judgment* of build-vs-buy and how the major providers fit mobile.

## The case for a managed provider
```text
Auth is SECURITY-CRITICAL and full of subtle, dangerous details:
  - secure password hashing, refresh-token rotation + reuse detection,
  - OAuth/PKCE flows, MFA, email/SMS verification, rate-limiting, breach response.
Getting ANY of these wrong is a vulnerability. Providers do them for you, audited and
maintained. For most apps, rolling your own auth is needless risk.
```
*Build your own only if you have a strong, specific reason* (unusual requirements, regulatory, full control) *and* the security expertise to own it. For the rest, buy.

## The major options (mobile-relevant notes)
```text
- Clerk        - excellent DX, drop-in React Native components, handles UI + sessions.
- Supabase Auth- open-source-friendly, integrates with a Supabase backend, good RN support.
- Firebase Auth- battle-tested, broad social providers, deep Google/Android integration.
- Auth0 / Okta - enterprise-grade, very configurable, common in larger orgs.
- AWS Cognito  - integrates with the AWS stack; powerful but rougher DX.
```
What to evaluate for *mobile* specifically:
```text
- First-class React Native / Expo SDK (not just a web SDK bolted on).
- Secure token storage on device + biometric integration.
- Social + Apple sign-in support (Apple's required-on-iOS rule, W14 D2).
- Deep-link handling for magic links / OAuth redirects (W14 D5).
- Pricing that scales sanely with your user count.
```

## You still own the integration
Even with a provider, *you* wire it correctly: store tokens in secure storage, handle the refresh lifecycle, manage deep-link redirects, add biometric gating, and handle logout/revocation. *A provider removes the cryptography and the flows; it doesn't remove your responsibility to integrate it securely.* The skills from this whole week are exactly what let you use a provider *well* rather than blindly.

Today: evaluate two providers against the mobile checklist for Hydra, and either *integrate* one (Clerk or Supabase have the smoothest Expo paths) replacing your hand-rolled pieces, *or* write a clear decision note on build-vs-buy with your reasoning. Knowing *when not to build* auth yourself is a senior judgment that prevents real security incidents.

## Ship it: Hydra v0.9, secure authentication
Package the week into **Hydra v0.9**: a complete, *secure* mobile auth system, sign-in, secure token storage, biometric unlock, OAuth, and deep-linked flows, the front door done to production standard.

## What v0.9 must demonstrate
- **Sign-in:** at least one real method (email/password or social via PKCE OAuth in a *secure system browser*, not a WebView), plus **Sign in with Apple** if you offer other social logins.
- **Secure token storage:** access + refresh tokens in `expo-secure-store` (Keychain/Keystore), *never* AsyncStorage; silent access-token mint on launch.
- **Biometric unlock:** Face ID/Touch ID/fingerprint gating an existing session ("logged in for months, but a glance to open").
- **Deep-linked auth flow:** a magic-link or email-confirmation (or OAuth redirect) that opens the app to the right screen, working from *cold start and warm*.
- **Clean logout/revocation:** clears secure storage *and* revokes server-side, with graceful forced-logout handling.

## Verify like a security reviewer
```text
[ ] Tokens are in SecureStore, NOT AsyncStorage (check storage)
[ ] OAuth uses the secure system browser + PKCE; NO client secret in the app
[ ] Log in once -> close -> reopen -> Face ID unlocks, no re-typed password
[ ] Magic/confirm link opens the app correctly from a COLD start (not just warm)
[ ] Logout revokes server-side; a revoked refresh -> clean logout, no retry loop
[ ] (If social) Sign in with Apple is offered (App Store rule)
```

```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Hydra v0.9: secure mobile auth (secure-store tokens, biometrics, PKCE OAuth, deep links)"
git push
```

You've built the front door *securely*, the part of an app where mistakes become breaches. Mobile auth's distinct challenges (no cookies, long sessions, biometrics, OAuth-in-a-browser, deep links) are now things you handle correctly. Next week: **background tasks and local notifications**, the heavily-restricted world of doing work when your app *isn't* in the foreground.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A user's access token expires while they are in the middle of using the app. How does the Axios interceptor handle this transparently? The interceptor catches the 401 response. It calls the refresh token endpoint with the stored refresh token. If the refresh succeeds, it gets a new access token, stores it in secure store, and retries the original request with the new token. From the user's perspective, the request that failed with 401 completes successfully a few hundred milliseconds later, they see no error. If the refresh fails (refresh token expired), the interceptor clears the stored tokens and redirects to the login screen.

weeks.title: Background Tasks and Local Notifications
weeks.context:
Background tasks on mobile are heavily restricted. The operating system aggressively kills background processes to preserve battery life. Understanding what you can and cannot do in the background is essential for building features that work reliably.

iOS background modes: apps can run in the background for specific, declared purposes: audio playback, location updates, background fetch, push content (VoIP, remote notifications with content-available). You declare these in app.json (UIBackgroundModes). Background fetch is the most generally useful, iOS allocates a short window (30 seconds) for your app to run when the OS decides to (typically when the device is charging, on Wi-Fi, and other apps are not actively using resources). You cannot control when this fires.

Android background tasks: more permissive than iOS but increasingly restricted in newer versions. WorkManager (the recommended Android background API) schedules deferrable, guaranteed background work. It respects battery optimisation, runs on device idle when connected to power, and guarantees execution even if the device reboots.

expo-task-manager wraps both platforms' background task systems. You define tasks with TaskManager.defineTask and trigger them with BackgroundFetch.registerTaskAsync (periodic) or Location.startGeofencingAsync (location-triggered). Tasks must complete within the allotted time.

Local notifications as background substitutes: for many "background task" use cases, scheduled local notifications are more reliable. Instead of running background code to check a condition and then show a notification, pre-schedule the notification at a known time. The OS delivers it without waking your app. For reminders (the W2 case), this is always the right approach.

Background fetch realistic expectations: iOS decides when to run background fetch. It uses adaptive scheduling based on how often your app's background fetch updates content that the user then accesses. If users frequently open the app right after a background fetch, iOS schedules it more often. If not, it schedules rarely or never. Do not build features that depend on reliable background fetch timing.

items.title: Orient, what you're building this week
items.body:
## Background work: the most restricted part of mobile
This week is **background tasks**, and the first thing to internalise is *how little you're allowed to do.* Unlike a server (which runs forever) or a web page (which at least runs while open), *mobile operating systems aggressively kill background work to save battery.* Your app does *not* get to run whenever it likes when backgrounded. Understanding *what you can and cannot do* is the whole game, building a feature on a false assumption about background execution is a guaranteed production failure.

## The core reality
```text
- iOS and Android KILL background processes aggressively to preserve battery.
- You CANNOT run arbitrary code continuously in the background. Full stop.
- What you CAN do is LIMITED, SCHEDULED, and OS-CONTROLLED:
    - brief, OS-granted "background fetch" windows (minutes apart, not guaranteed),
    - reacting to PUSH (the server wakes you - W11),
    - specific declared modes (audio, navigation/location, VoIP),
    - LOCAL NOTIFICATIONS the OS fires on your behalf (no code needed at fire time).
- The OS decides WHEN (and IF) your background task runs, based on battery, usage
  patterns, and system load. "Every 15 minutes" really means "maybe, sometimes, when
  the OS feels like it."
```
*Design for "best effort, eventually", not "guaranteed, on time".* An app that *depends* on precise background execution will fail for real users.

## The right mental model: who does the work?
```text
- Needs to happen at an EXACT time, reliably? -> a LOCAL NOTIFICATION (OS fires it) or
  a SERVER push (W11). Don't rely on your code running in the background to do it.
- Periodic "refresh data when convenient"? -> background fetch (best-effort window).
- Heavy/scheduled work that must be reliable? -> do it on a SERVER, push the result.
```
The recurring lesson: *push reliable, time-critical work to the OS (notifications) or the server, and treat your own background execution as opportunistic.*

## This week's arc
You'll learn iOS **background modes** (what's allowed, D2), **background-fetch** (opportunistic periodic work, D3), rich **notification actions** (D4), **background location** (the heaviest, most-scrutinised mode, D5), and Android's **WorkManager** (the modern background scheduler, D6).

Today, orient: install `expo-task-manager` and `expo-background-fetch`, register a trivial background-fetch task that logs a timestamp, and observe, over a while, how *irregularly* the OS actually runs it. Feeling that "the OS decides, not me" is the foundational lesson of background work.

items.title: iOS background modes
items.body:
## iOS background modes: what you're actually allowed to do
iOS is *strict* about background execution: an app can only do background work for *specific, declared purposes*. You declare these **background modes** in `app.json`, and *using one without a legitimate matching feature gets your app rejected.* Knowing the allowed modes, and which one (if any) fits your feature, is today's job.

## The declared background modes
```text
UIBackgroundModes (declared in app.json / Info.plist), the main ones:
- audio            - play audio in the background (music/podcast apps).
- location         - continuous location updates (navigation, fitness tracking).
- fetch            - periodic background app refresh (opportunistic, brief).
- remote-notification - wake on a silent push to fetch content (W11 silent push).
- processing       - longer maintenance tasks, run when the device is idle/charging.
- voip             - voice-over-IP apps.
```
Each mode is a *promise to Apple* about why you run in the background, and Apple checks that your app actually has the matching feature. *Declaring `location` without a real location feature, or `audio` without playing audio, is a rejection.*

## The honest question for every "background" feature
```text
1. Does a declared mode ACTUALLY cover my use case? (Often: no.)
2. Could a LOCAL NOTIFICATION do it instead? (Fixed-time reminders -> yes.)
3. Could a SERVER PUSH do it instead? (Server-known events -> yes.)
4. Could it just run NEXT TIME the app opens? (Most "sync" -> yes.)
```
Most features developers *think* need background execution actually need a *notification*, a *push*, or *foreground catch-up*. Reaching for a background mode is the exception, and an unjustified one is an App Store problem.

## Background time is brief and revocable
Even with a valid mode, you get *limited* time and the OS can *suspend* you mid-task:
```text
- Background fetch windows are SHORT (seconds) and INFREQUENT (OS-decided).
- The OS suspends/kills you if you overstay or the system is under pressure.
- An app the user rarely opens gets LESS background time (iOS learns usage patterns).
```
So background tasks must be *quick, idempotent, and resumable*, do a little, save progress, and be fine with being cut off. *Never assume a background task runs to completion.*

Today: for Hydra, decide honestly whether *any* feature needs a declared background mode (a hydration *reminder* almost certainly wants a *local notification*, not background code). Declare only what's justified in `app.json`, and write the one-line justification you'd give Apple for each mode you keep. Choosing *not* to over-claim background modes is the mark of someone who understands iOS.

items.title: Notification categories and actions on iOS
items.body:
## Notification actions: making notifications interactive
A notification doesn't have to be a passive banner. **Notification categories and actions** let users *act directly from the notification*, buttons like "Log 250 ml" or "Snooze" right on the banner or lock screen, without opening the app. This is high-value mobile UX, and a great example of doing useful work *around* the background-execution limits.

## Categories and actions
You define a **category** (a type of notification) with **actions** (buttons), then attach that category to notifications you send:
```tsx
import * as Notifications from 'expo-notifications';

await Notifications.setNotificationCategoryAsync('hydration-reminder', [
  { identifier: 'log-250', buttonTitle: 'Log 250 ml' },
  { identifier: 'snooze',  buttonTitle: 'Snooze 30m' },
]);

// when scheduling/sending, set categoryIdentifier: 'hydration-reminder'
```
The OS renders those buttons on the notification. When the user taps one, your app receives the action *identifier* and responds:
```tsx
Notifications.addNotificationResponseReceivedListener(res => {
  if (res.actionIdentifier === 'log-250') logWater(250);   // act WITHOUT opening the app UI
  if (res.actionIdentifier === 'snooze')  rescheduleIn(30);
});
```

## Why this is powerful (and the limits)
```text
- Users complete an action in ONE TAP from the lock screen -> huge UX win, real
  re-engagement (logging water is now frictionless).
- The handler runs with LIMITED background time -> keep the work QUICK (write locally,
  queue a sync via W13's offline queue; don't try a long network call here).
- Foreground (text-entry) actions exist too (e.g. quick-reply), iOS/Android differ in
  capability; test on both.
```
This pairs perfectly with the offline-sync pattern: the action *writes locally and queues*, so it works instantly even with no signal, and syncs later.

## Platform differences
```text
- iOS: categories + actions; some actions can show a text field; "destructive"/
  "authentication-required" flags exist.
- Android: actions on notifications too, tied to channels (W11 D3); behaviour and
  styling differ. Test BOTH - notification UX is one of the least faithful in emulators.
```

Today: add interactive actions to Hydra's reminder notification, a "Log 250 ml" button that records the entry (locally + queued) *without* opening the app, and a "Snooze" that reschedules. Verify on a real device that tapping the button logs water from the lock screen. One-tap actions turn a reminder from a nag into a feature.

items.title: Background location
items.body:
## Background location: the heaviest, most-scrutinised capability
**Background location**, tracking the user's location when the app is closed, is the *most powerful* and *most restricted* background capability. It enables real features (fitness run-tracking, geofencing, navigation) but at a steep cost in battery, privacy, and App Store scrutiny. Today is about using it *only when justified*, and *correctly* when you do.

## Why it's special (and watched)
```text
- It's a declared background MODE (location) AND needs "Always Allow" permission (W10).
- It DRAINS BATTERY - continuous GPS is one of the biggest battery costs on a phone.
- It's the most PRIVACY-SENSITIVE data there is (W10 D6) - a trail of where someone goes.
- Apple/Google SCRUTINISE it hard: you must justify it with a visible feature, and
  iOS periodically reminds the user you've been using their location in the background.
```
*The bar for using background location is high*, and rightly so. Most apps that *think* they need it actually need *geofencing* (the OS notifies you on boundary crossing, far cheaper) rather than *continuous* tracking.

## The two background-location patterns
```text
1. GEOFENCING (W10 D5) - register regions; the OS wakes you on enter/exit.
   Battery-cheap because YOU don't run GPS - the OS notifies you. Prefer this.
2. CONTINUOUS background updates - you receive a stream of locations while backgrounded
   (a fitness app tracing a run). EXPENSIVE; justified only for active tracking features.
```
```tsx
import * as Location from 'expo-location';
import * as TaskManager from 'expo-task-manager';

TaskManager.defineTask('bg-location', ({ data }) => {
  const { locations } = data;             // batched location updates
  // persist locally (W8) + queue sync (W13); keep it light
});

await Location.startLocationUpdatesAsync('bg-location', {
  accuracy: Location.Accuracy.Balanced,   // lower accuracy = less battery
  deferredUpdatesInterval: 60_000,        // batch updates to save power
  showsBackgroundLocationIndicator: true, // honesty: the user SEES it's active
});
```

## Battery discipline is mandatory
```text
- Use the LOWEST accuracy that works; high accuracy = battery murder.
- BATCH updates (deferred intervals) instead of a constant high-frequency stream.
- STOP tracking the moment the feature is done (run ended) - don't leave GPS running.
- Prefer significant-change / geofencing over continuous where possible.
```
*A background-location feature that drains the battery gets uninstalled, and reviewed badly.* Efficiency isn't optional; it's the feature working acceptably.

Today: decide honestly whether Hydra needs *any* background location (it likely needs only the W10 *geofence*, not continuous tracking) and either implement an *efficient* continuous-tracking demo (low accuracy, batched, with the background indicator, stopping when done) *or* write the justification for why geofencing suffices. Choosing the *cheaper* capability that meets the need is the expert move.

items.title: Workmanager on Android (the modern background scheduler)
items.body:
## Android background work: WorkManager and the modern scheduler
Android's background-execution story is *different* from iOS's and has its own modern solution: **WorkManager**, the recommended API for *deferrable, guaranteed* background work. Understanding how Android approaches background tasks, and how it differs from iOS, completes your background picture (and explains some cross-platform behaviour differences).

## Android's background evolution
Android historically allowed *more* background freedom than iOS, then progressively *clamped down* (Doze mode, App Standby, background limits) to fix the battery drain that freedom caused:
```text
- Doze mode: when the device is idle/stationary, Android BATCHES and DEFERS background
  work into periodic "maintenance windows" to save battery.
- App Standby: apps the user rarely touches get their background work throttled.
- Background execution limits: background SERVICES are heavily restricted on modern Android.
```
The result: like iOS, modern Android does *not* let you run freely in the background, *the platforms have converged on "the OS controls background work for battery's sake."*

## WorkManager: the right tool for deferrable work
**WorkManager** is Android's modern API for background tasks that should run *eventually and reliably*, even surviving app restarts and device reboots:
```text
- Use for: DEFERRABLE, GUARANTEED work (sync this data eventually, upload this log,
  periodic cleanup). NOT for exact-time or real-time work.
- It respects Doze/Standby and runs work in batched maintenance windows.
- It supports CONSTRAINTS: "only on Wi-Fi", "only while charging", "only when network
  available" - so you do heavy/expensive work at the RIGHT time.
- It GUARANTEES execution (eventually) and survives reboot - stronger than iOS's
  best-effort fetch.
```
In Expo, background-fetch / task-manager abstract over the platform specifics (WorkManager-like scheduling on Android, BGTaskScheduler on iOS), so you often write *one* task and Expo maps it, but knowing WorkManager is underneath explains the Android behaviour and constraints.

## The cross-platform takeaway
```text
- iOS: background fetch = OPPORTUNISTIC, brief, not guaranteed.
- Android (WorkManager): deferrable work = GUARANTEED eventually, with constraints,
  survives reboot - but STILL deferred (Doze), not real-time.
- BOTH: real-time/exact-time -> use notifications or push, not background code.
- BOTH: respect battery; use constraints (Wi-Fi/charging) for heavy work.
```

Today: review how Hydra's background work behaves on *Android* specifically (test on a real Android device: does the fetch/sync run, and how does Doze affect it?), and write a short note contrasting iOS background-fetch (opportunistic) with Android WorkManager (guaranteed-but-deferred, constraint-aware). Understanding *both* platforms' models is what lets you build background features that actually work cross-platform.
