items.title: Ship it
items.body:
## Ship it: Hydra v0.10, background-aware
Package the week into **Hydra v0.10**: background and notification features that work *within* the platforms' strict limits, opportunistic refresh, interactive notifications, and an honest, battery-respecting posture toward background work. The mark of success here is *restraint done right*, not over-claiming background powers.

## What v0.10 must demonstrate
- **Honest background modes:** only the modes Hydra genuinely justifies declared in `app.json` (most likely *none* beyond what a reminder needs), each with a one-line justification.
- **Opportunistic background fetch:** a quick, idempotent refresh task, *and* proof the app works perfectly if it never runs.
- **Interactive notifications:** a reminder with a one-tap "Log 250 ml" action that records the entry (locally + queued) *without* opening the app, plus "Snooze".
- **Background location handled correctly:** either an *efficient* (low-accuracy, batched, indicator-on, stops-when-done) tracking demo, *or* a justification for using geofencing instead.
- **Cross-platform awareness:** verified behaviour on *both* iOS and a real Android (Doze/WorkManager differences understood).

## Verify like a reviewer
```text
[ ] Only JUSTIFIED background modes declared (no over-claiming -> App Store safe)
[ ] App works fully even if background fetch NEVER runs (it's an optimisation)
[ ] Notification action logs water from the lock screen (quick, queued, no app open)
[ ] Any background location is low-accuracy + batched + stops when done (battery)
[ ] Tested on real iOS AND real Android (background behaviour differs)
```

```bash
git add . && git commit -m "Hydra v0.10: background-aware (justified modes, fetch, notification actions, battery-respecting)"
git push
```

You've learned the *most counterintuitive* area of mobile: you don't control the background, the OS does, and the skill is doing useful work *within* those limits while pushing reliable, time-critical work to notifications and the server. Restraint and honesty here are what keep your app efficient and App-Store-approved. Next week: **analytics, crash reporting, and observability**, getting *evidence* of how your app behaves in the wild instead of guessing.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You want to sync Hydra's habit completions to a server every hour in the background. Can you rely on expo-background-fetch for this? No. Background fetch is unreliable for scheduled, time-critical tasks. iOS decides when to run it based on its own heuristics, it may run every hour or once a day. The reliable alternative: when the user makes a change (checks off a habit), sync immediately in the foreground. If the sync fails (offline), queue it locally (SQLite with a synced=false flag) and retry when the app next comes to the foreground (AppState active event). Background fetch can be used as an opportunistic sync to catch anything missed, but not as the primary sync mechanism.

weeks.title: Analytics, Crash Reporting, and Observability
weeks.context:
Mobile analytics and crash reporting are not optional for a production app. Without them, you find out about crashes from App Store reviews, and you find out about user behaviour patterns when you guess. With them, you have evidence.

Crash reporting: Sentry is the standard. It captures unhandled JavaScript errors, native crashes (in development builds), the stack trace, the device model and OS version, the user's session, and groups duplicate crashes. One crash affecting 500 users appears as one Sentry issue with a count of 500. Without Sentry, it looks like no reported bugs. Install @sentry/react-native and initialise it before your root component renders.

Analytics: you need to know how users move through your app. Which screens do they visit? Where do they drop off in the onboarding flow? What features do the retained users use? Mixpanel, Amplitude, or PostHog are the standard mobile analytics tools. You instrument events manually: track('habit_checked', { habitId, habitName, completionStreak }). The events you do not instrument are invisible. Instrument the most important user actions on day one, not later.

Event taxonomy: design your events deliberately before you start tracking. Events have a verb-noun format: habit_completed, habit_created, habit_deleted, onboarding_completed, reminder_set, notification_opened. Include properties that allow segmentation: which habit, what time of day, what device, what app version. An event with no properties tells you something happened but not why or in what context.

Performance monitoring: track app startup time, screen render time, and API response times. Sentry's performance monitoring and Expo's built-in performance tools measure these. App startup time directly affects Day 1 retention, apps that take more than 3 seconds to show content lose a measurable percentage of new users.

Privacy and consent: analytics tracking requires user consent in the EU (GDPR) and increasingly in other jurisdictions. On iOS 14.5+, ATT (App Tracking Transparency) requires explicit user permission for cross-app tracking. For first-party analytics (tracking your own users in your own app), ATT does not apply. But if you use advertising networks or cross-device tracking, ATT consent is required.

weeks.title: Building for Performance, Bundles, Frames, Memory
weeks.context:
60 frames per second is the contract between your app and your users. At 60fps, animations feel smooth and interactions feel instant. At 30fps, everything feels slightly sluggish. Below 30fps, the app feels broken. Performance problems on mobile have different causes than on web, and fixing them requires understanding how React Native renders.

The render pipeline: React renders to a virtual DOM diff, passes the diff to the React Native bridge (or JSI), which calls native layout and drawing APIs. The result is displayed on screen. This pipeline runs on every state update. The JavaScript thread handles your React renders, event handlers, and business logic. The UI thread handles native rendering. They run concurrently, JavaScript being slow does not directly cause dropped frames, but passing too much work across the bridge can.

The most common performance problems: re-rendering components that did not change, computing expensive values on every render, rendering large lists inefficiently, and passing large data across the bridge too frequently.

React DevTools profiler: shows which components re-rendered and how long each render took. Accessible via the Expo Dev Tools. Use it to identify the "hot" components, the ones that re-render most often and take the longest.

Memoisation: React.memo wraps a component and only re-renders when its props change (shallow equality check). useMemo caches the result of a computation and only recomputes when dependencies change. useCallback caches a function reference and only creates a new function when dependencies change. Overusing these adds complexity, use them only when the React Profiler shows that a component is re-rendering unnecessarily and the re-render is expensive.

FlatList optimisations: getItemLayout tells FlatList the exact height of each item, so it does not need to measure them. initialNumToRender controls how many items render on the first pass. windowSize controls how many screens of content are rendered above and below the visible area. removeClippedSubviews offloads off-screen items from memory (experimental, may cause issues, test carefully).

Hermes is the JavaScript engine used in modern React Native. It is optimised for mobile: it compiles JavaScript to bytecode at build time (instead of JIT at runtime), which significantly reduces startup time. It is enabled by default in Expo SDK 47+.

weeks.title: Accessibility, Building for Everyone
weeks.context:
Mobile accessibility is about building apps that work for the 15-20% of users who have visual, motor, or cognitive disabilities. Screen readers, large text, reduced motion, and switch access are not edge cases, they are features that millions of users depend on daily. App stores increasingly require accessibility compliance, and enterprise app buyers evaluate it in their procurement criteria.

VoiceOver (iOS) and TalkBack (Android) are the built-in screen readers. They read aloud the content and purpose of every UI element as the user navigates with swipe gestures (or on Android, touch exploration). A properly accessible app works completely eyes-free. Test your app with VoiceOver enabled (iOS: Settings > Accessibility > VoiceOver > On, or triple-click the side button). Navigate using swipe right/left to move between elements, double-tap to activate.

The accessibility API in React Native: accessible={true} marks an element as a single accessible unit. accessibilityLabel="Check off morning run" provides the text VoiceOver reads. accessibilityHint="Double tap to check or uncheck" provides additional context. accessibilityRole="button" tells the screen reader what type of element it is ('button', 'checkbox', 'header', 'image', 'text', 'link'). accessibilityState={{ checked: isCompleted }} communicates state.

Accessible names: if an element has only an icon (no text label), it is invisible to screen readers without an accessibilityLabel. A button with a trash icon and no label is announced as "image" or nothing. Add accessibilityLabel="Delete habit" to icon-only buttons.

Text scaling: users set a preferred text size in OS settings. On iOS, this affects all apps that use Dynamic Type. React Native Text components scale with system font size by default. Test at the largest text size (Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Larger Text > max). Layout must not break, buttons must stay tappable, text must not be clipped.

Reduced motion: some users experience vestibular disorders and get motion sickness from animations. iOS and Android have a "Reduce Motion" setting. Read it with AccessibilityInfo.isReduceMotionEnabled() and disable or simplify animations for these users.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have a habit row component. VoiceOver reads "Morning run, image, button, button", the user hears four separate things when they swipe through the row. What should it say and how do you fix it? It should say "Morning run, completed, double tap to toggle" (one thing). Wrap the entire row in a View with accessible={true}. The accessible prop makes the view a single accessibility element, VoiceOver treats it as one unit. Add accessibilityLabel="Morning run" and accessibilityState={{ checked: isCompleted }}. Add accessibilityHint="Double tap to toggle completion". With this setup, VoiceOver reads the whole row as one element with complete information.

weeks.title: Internationalisation, Multiple Languages, Currencies, Dates
weeks.context:
Internationalisation (i18n) is preparing your app to support multiple languages, regions, and locales. Localisation (l10n) is adapting the app for a specific locale. Most apps need both if they are targeting international markets. Even for English-only apps, you should understand date, number, and currency formatting differences.

i18n-js and i18next are the standard libraries. They manage translation strings, handle pluralisation rules (English: 1 item, 2 items; Arabic: has 6 plural forms), interpolate variables into translated strings, and fall back to a default language when a translation is missing.

Translation files: you maintain one JSON file per locale, with the same key structure. en.json: { "habit_count": "{{count}} habits" }, ar.json: { "habit_count": "{{count}} عادة" }. Your code references keys, never hardcoded strings: t('habit_count', { count: habits.length }).

Locale detection: on mobile, the device locale (the language/region the user has set in their OS settings) is available from expo-localization. Expo.getLocales() returns an ordered list of the user's preferred locales. Use the first one as your app's locale if it is supported, otherwise fall back to your default.

Number and currency formatting: 1,234.56 in the US is 1.234,56 in Germany and 1 234,56 in France. Use Intl.NumberFormat (built into the JavaScript engine) with the locale: new Intl.NumberFormat('de-DE', { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' }).format(1234.56). Never hardcode number separators.

Date and time formatting: July 4 is 4 Juli in German, 4 luglio in Italian. Use Intl.DateTimeFormat for localised date strings. Also consider: some locales use right-to-left (RTL) text direction, Arabic, Hebrew, Persian. React Native has RTL support (I18nManager.forceRTL) but it requires testing and thoughtful layout decisions (margins and paddings swap, icon positions swap, text alignment changes).

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have the string "You have completed 1 habit today." When there are 2 habits, it should say "2 habits." When 0, "0 habits." How do you handle this with i18next? Use i18next's pluralisation. In your translation file: { "habits_completed": "You have completed {{count}} habit today", "habits_completed_plural": "You have completed {{count}} habits today", "habits_completed_zero": "You have not completed any habits today" }. In your code: t('habits_completed', { count: completedCount }). i18next selects the correct key based on the count and the locale's pluralisation rules. In English, _zero overrides count=0, _plural applies to count>=2. In a language with 6 plural forms (Arabic), you would provide 6 keys.

weeks.title: Testing, Unit, Component, E2E on Mobile
weeks.context:
Testing mobile apps is harder than testing web apps. You have two platforms (iOS and Android), two test environments (simulator and device), hardware variations, OS version fragmentation, and device-specific behaviours. A test strategy that ignores this complexity will miss platform-specific bugs. A test strategy that tries to cover everything will be too slow to run.

Unit testing in React Native uses Jest (bundled with Expo). Pure functions (streak calculation, date formatting, validation logic) are easy to test with Jest, they have no dependencies on React Native or the device. Test these aggressively. For React components, use @testing-library/react-native, it renders components in a virtual environment and allows querying by accessible labels, text, and roles.

Component tests with @testing-library/react-native: use getByRole, getByLabelText, and getByText to find elements (the same queries used by screen readers, which also confirms accessibility). Use fireEvent to simulate user interactions. Use waitFor to handle async operations. These tests run in Node without a device and are fast.

Mocking native modules: most React Native native modules cannot run in Jest's Node environment (they call native code). Mock them: jest.mock('expo-secure-store', () => ({ getItemAsync: jest.fn(), setItemAsync: jest.fn() })). Expo provides a jest-preset that mocks many Expo modules automatically. Use jest-expo preset in your Jest config.

End-to-end testing with Detox: Detox runs a real app on a simulator/device and drives it like a user (tap, type, swipe). It uses a grey box approach, it knows when your app is idle (no JS work pending, no animations running) and only proceeds when the app is ready. This makes Detox tests significantly more stable than naive timeout-based E2E tests. Detox is complex to set up but essential for testing critical user flows (sign up, first habit creation, subscription).

Test coverage strategy: unit tests for all business logic, component tests for interactive components (forms, lists), integration tests for screens that involve navigation and API calls (mocked), and Detox E2E for 3-5 critical user journeys. Do not aim for line coverage, aim for critical path coverage.

weeks.title: EAS Build and Submit, Shipping to Stores
weeks.context:
Expo Application Services (EAS) is Expo's cloud build and submission service. It replaces the complex native build setup with a managed cloud service that builds your app on Apple's macOS infrastructure (for iOS) and Linux (for Android). The result is a signed .ipa (iOS) or .aab (Android) file ready for store submission.

EAS Build: you define build profiles in eas.json (development, preview, production). A development build is installed on your device and connected to the Metro bundler for hot reload. A preview build is a standalone app (no Metro connection) for testing. A production build is what you submit to the stores. Run eas build --platform all --profile production to build for both stores simultaneously.

Code signing is the biggest complexity in mobile deployment. iOS requires: a bundle ID registered in Apple Developer portal, a provisioning profile (which devices are allowed to install the app), and a distribution certificate. EAS manages all of this with eas credentials, it generates and stores the certificates for you. Android requires: a keystore (a cryptographic key that signs your APK). EAS generates and securely stores your keystore. Never lose your keystore, you cannot update your Android app without the same keystore used to sign the original.

EAS Submit: after a successful build, eas submit --platform ios submits the .ipa to App Store Connect, and eas submit --platform android submits the .aab to Google Play. This replaces manually downloading the build and uploading it through the web dashboards. Requires API keys for both stores.

Over-the-Air (OTA) updates: for JavaScript-only changes (no native code changes), you do not need to submit a new build to the stores. EAS Update deploys a new JavaScript bundle to your app's update channel. weeks.title: Updates, Versioning, and OTA
weeks.context:
App versioning and update strategy are the operational concerns that determine how smoothly you can ship changes to users. Unlike web (where you deploy once and all users are immediately on the new version), mobile apps have version fragmentation, users on version 1.0 coexist with users on 1.2 and 1.5. Your backend must handle requests from all live versions.

Semantic versioning for mobile: version (user-visible: 1.2.3, shown in the store) and buildNumber/versionCode (internal counter, incremented with every submitted build). The store rejects builds with a duplicate versionCode. Conventions: major version for breaking changes, minor for new features, patch for bug fixes. Build numbers go 1, 2, 3... or use YYYYMMDDNN format (2026052601).

API versioning: your mobile app talks to your API. When you change the API (remove a field, change a response format), old app versions break. Solutions: version your API (/api/v1/habits). Keep v1 running while deploying v2. Old app versions hit v1, new versions hit v2. Deprecate v1 gradually. The alternative is to design APIs that are additive only, never remove fields, only add new ones (but give old fields a deprecatedAt marker and log their usage).

Forced updates: sometimes you must force users to update (a critical security vulnerability, an API deprecation). Implement a minimum app version check: your server returns the minimum required version (1.1.0) and the current user's app version (from expo-constants). If below minimum, show a non-dismissable update screen with a link to the store.

Update channels with EAS: EAS Update uses channels (main, production, staging) and branches (like git branches). You publish an update to a channel and all app builds pointing to that channel receive it. You can roll back to a previous update by republishing an older update to the channel. This is your escape hatch when an OTA update has a bug.

Changelog and release notes: App Store and Google Play ask for "What's New" with every update. Write it for users, not developers. "Fixed a bug where streaks were calculated incorrectly" is good. "Fix off-by-one error in streakCalculator.ts" is developer-speak.

concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You push an OTA update that has a bug, the habits list crashes on load. 30% of your users have already received the update. How do you roll back? In EAS Update, publish a rollback: eas update --branch production --republish to republish the last known-good update to the production channel. Users who received the buggy update will download the rollback on their next app open. For the 30% currently on the buggy version: if the crash prevents the app from opening (and So downloading the rollback), you cannot reach them with OTA. This is why you test OTA updates on a preview channel first before publishing to production.

weeks.title: App Store Optimisation, Getting Found and Installed
weeks.context:
App Store Optimisation (ASO) is to the App Store what SEO is to Google, the practice of making your app more discoverable and compelling to potential users. Most app installs come from App Store search. The factors that determine whether your app appears and whether users download it are within your control.

The App Store search algorithm: keyword relevance, conversion rate (how many people who see your app install it), ratings and reviews (both count and recency), and engagement (how often users open the app after installing). Your job: optimise the first three. Engagement comes from building a good app.

Keyword research: find the words and phrases your target users search for. Tools: AppFollow, Sensor Tower, MobileAction, or the free AppFollow free tier. Search for your app's use case and look at what apps rank. Your app's title, subtitle, and keywords field contribute to search ranking. The title is weighted highest. The keywords field accepts up to 100 characters (comma-separated, no spaces around commas). Do not repeat words from the title in the keywords, they are already indexed.

Screenshots are the most important conversion factor. On the search results page, users see your first 1-3 screenshots (depending on the device) before tapping. These screenshots decide whether they tap to learn more. Best practice: the first screenshot conveys the core value proposition with a short caption. Subsequent screenshots show the key features. Use a device frame with marketing text (tools: Rottenwood, AppLaunchpad, or Figma templates). Test different screenshot sets with App Store A/B testing (Apple's Product Page Optimization).

Ratings and reviews: users who love your app rarely leave reviews unless prompted. Use expo-store-review (which calls SKStoreReviewAPI on iOS and its Android equivalent) to show the native rating prompt at the right moment, after the user has had a positive experience (after a habit streak milestone, after they explicitly say they enjoy the app). The rating prompt can only be shown 3 times per year per user. Choose the moment wisely.

Respond to every review, especially negative ones. A thoughtful response to a 1-star review shows potential users that you care. "We are sorry to hear this, please email support@hydra.app and we will resolve this for you" turns a public complaint into an invitation to fix the problem privately.

weeks.title: Capstone, Ship to Both Stores, Real Users
weeks.context:
This is the week you ship Hydra to both the App Store and Google Play and get your first real users. The capstone is not about adding features, it is about going through the full release cycle: review preparation, submission, approval, and distribution. And then doing the harder thing: getting real people to install and use the app.

App Store review takes 1-3 days on average. The review team checks: does the app crash? Does it do what the description says? Are all features accessible (not behind broken paywall logic)? Does it comply with the App Store guidelines (no unapproved content, no privacy violations, no misleading interface)? Google Play review takes a few hours to a few days.

Pre-submission checklist: the app does not crash on first launch or during normal use. All screens are accessible via VoiceOver/TalkBack. The app has a privacy policy URL (required if you collect any data). Permission usage descriptions are in app.json (NSCameraUsageDescription, NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription, etc.) and match the actual permissions used. The app icon has no alpha channel (App Store requirement). Screenshots are in the correct sizes for all device types.

Review notes: when submitting, you can add notes to the reviewer. If your app has any unusual features or requires specific steps to test, explain them. If your app requires a login, provide a test account. If a feature requires a specific hardware (like Face ID), describe what the reviewer will see on a device without it.

After launch: the real work begins. Track your crash rate (Sentry), rating (AppFollow), and installs (App Store Connect, Google Play Console). The first week of data tells you a lot about onboarding, where users drop off is where you iterate first. Respond to every review. Fix every crash.

Getting your first users: post in relevant communities (r/habits, r/getdisciplined, r/productivityapps on Reddit, IndieHackers, Product Hunt). Share your launch story, how you built it, what you learned, why you built it. The authentic builder story is more compelling than a generic launch post. Write a blog post about building Hydra in 24 weeks.
